lessons.title: How a database stores and finds rows
lessons.intro:
A query describes the rows you want. The database has to go and find them on disk. This module shows what is on the disk, what reading it costs, and why that cost decides whether a query is fast.

The course uses PostgreSQL for its examples, because the SQL course in this app runs on it. Other relational databases use different names and details for the same ideas.

steps.title: Tables are files of pages
steps.text:
A table is stored as a file. The file is divided into fixed-size blocks called **pages**, 8 KB each in PostgreSQL. Each page holds as many rows as fit, often between 50 and 200.

The database never reads one row from disk. It reads the whole page that contains it. So the cost of a query is counted in pages read, not in rows returned.

Rows in a table are in no particular order. A new row goes wherever there is free space. A table stored this way is called a **heap**.

steps.title: Reading every page
steps.text:
Suppose you ask for one order by its ID and the table has no index. The database has no way to know which page holds it. It reads every page from the first to the last and checks every row. This is a **sequential scan**, also called a full table scan.

Its cost grows with the size of the table. A table of 1,000 rows fits in about 10 pages, and scanning it is instant. A table of 100 million rows is about a million pages, or 8 GB. Reading all of it to return one row takes seconds.

That is the usual story behind "it was fast in testing and slow in production". The query did not change. The table grew.

A sequential scan is not always wrong. When a query needs a large share of the table, reading every page in order is the cheapest way to get it.

steps.title: Memory and disk
steps.text:
Reading a page from disk is slow compared with reading it from memory. So the database keeps recently used pages in memory, in an area called the **buffer cache** (in PostgreSQL, shared buffers).

- A page found in the cache costs almost nothing.
- A page that must be read from disk costs far more: around 0.1 ms on a fast disk, and much longer on a slow or busy one.

This explains a pattern you will see often. A query is slow the first time and fast the second, because the first run brought its pages into memory. It also explains why a database slows sharply when its commonly used data stops fitting in memory.

steps.title: Twice in a row
steps.text: A report query runs for 14 seconds. Someone runs the same query again a moment later, and it takes 0.9 seconds. Nothing was changed in between.

steps.title: What a row looks like
steps.text:
Each row is stored with a small header and then its column values. Two details matter for design.

- **Row width.** Narrow rows mean more rows per page, so fewer pages to read. A table with 30 wide columns is slower to scan than one with 6, even when a query uses only two of them, because whole rows are stored together.
- **Large values are moved out.** A long text or JSON value does not fit in a page with other rows. PostgreSQL stores such values in a separate area and keeps a pointer in the row. Reading the row is cheap. Reading the large value costs extra page reads.

This is why `SELECT *` is a poor habit in application code. It fetches every column, including large ones the code never looks at.

steps.title: Changing a row
steps.text:
PostgreSQL does not overwrite a row when you update it. It writes a new version of the row and marks the old version as no longer current. A delete only marks the row. The space is reclaimed later by a background process.

Two consequences follow, and both come back in later modules.

- Readers are not blocked by writers. A query that started earlier can keep reading the old version while a new one is written.
- Old versions take up space until they are cleaned up. A table that is updated heavily can grow far larger than its live data. This is called **bloat**.

steps.title: The log that makes changes safe
steps.text:
Writing changed pages straight to the table files would be slow, and a crash in the middle would leave them half written. So the database first appends a short record of each change to a file called the **write-ahead log** (WAL). A change counts as saved once its log record is on disk.

Appending to one file is fast, since it is a single sequential write. The changed pages are written to the table files later, in the background. After a crash, the database replays the log to rebuild whatever had not reached the table files.

The same log does two more jobs. It is what replicas read to stay in step, and it is what makes it possible to restore a backup to an exact moment.

steps.title: Count the pages
steps.text: A table has 20 million rows, about 100 rows per page. A query asks for the 3 rows with `customer_id = 5521`. There is no index on that column.

steps.title: Exercise: explain the slowdown
steps.text:
A team reports three things about an `events` table that has grown from 50,000 to 80 million rows over two years.

1. "Finding one event by its ID used to take 2 ms and now takes 9 seconds."
2. "The nightly report is slow on Monday morning and fast for the rest of the day."
3. "The table holds 80 million rows and takes up 140 GB, though a row is only about 300 bytes."

Explain each one using the ideas in this module. For the third, estimate what size you would expect.

steps.title: One possible answer
steps.text:
1. **A sequential scan on a table that grew.** There is no usable index on the ID, so the database reads every page. At 50,000 rows that was a few hundred pages. At 80 million it is millions. The fix is an index, which is the next module.
2. **A cold cache.** Over the weekend the pages this report needs were pushed out of memory by other work, or the server was restarted. The first run reads them from disk. Later runs find them in the buffer cache.
3. **Bloat.** 80 million rows at 300 bytes is about 24 GB, and with page overhead perhaps 30 GB. The table is more than four times that. Rows in it are updated or deleted often, and the old versions are not being cleaned up fast enough. Indexes add size as well, though the question was about the table alone.

All three have the same root. The cost of a query is the number of pages it must read, and how many of those are already in memory.

questions.prompt: What is the most likely reason?

choices.text: The database stored the result of the first run
choices.feedback: PostgreSQL does not keep query results. It ran the whole query again.

choices.text: The pages the query reads were on disk the first time and in memory the second
choices.feedback: The first run paid for the disk reads and left the pages in the buffer cache. The work is the same. Only the cost per page changed.

choices.text: The second run used a better plan
choices.feedback: Nothing changed that would produce a different plan.

questions.prompt: About how many pages does the database read?

choices.text: 3, one for each matching row
choices.feedback: Without an index it cannot know which pages hold those rows.

choices.text: About 100
choices.feedback: That is the number of rows in one page, not the number of pages.

choices.text: About 200,000, the whole table
choices.feedback: 20 million rows at 100 per page is 200,000 pages. Every one is read to find 3 rows.

lessons.title: Indexes
lessons.intro: An index lets the database go straight to the rows it needs without reading the whole table. This module covers how the usual kind of index is built, which questions it can answer, and what every index costs.

steps.title: What an index is
steps.text:
An **index** is a separate structure, stored beside the table, that holds the values of one or more columns in sorted order. Next to each value it holds the location of the row: the page and the position in it.

It works like the index at the back of a book. The index is sorted, so a word is found quickly, and next to it is the page number to turn to.

The table itself is unchanged. An index is a second copy of some columns, arranged for searching.

```sql
CREATE INDEX orders_customer_id_idx ON orders (customer_id);
```

steps.title: The B-tree
steps.text:
The standard index is a **B-tree**. It is a tree of pages.

- The **leaf pages** at the bottom hold every indexed value in sorted order, each with the location of its row. The leaves are linked to each other, left to right.
- The pages above them hold signposts: "values below 5000 are down this branch".
- The **root** is the single page at the top.

To find a value, the database starts at the root and follows one signpost per level down to a leaf. The tree is wide and shallow. Each page holds hundreds of entries, so three or four levels are enough for hundreds of millions of rows.

That is the whole point. A lookup reads three or four index pages and then one table page, however large the table is.

steps.title: What a B-tree can answer
steps.text:
Since the leaves are sorted and linked, a B-tree serves more than exact matches.

| Query | Uses the index? | How |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `WHERE id = 42` | Yes | Walk down to one leaf entry |
| `WHERE created_at >= '2025-01-01'` | Yes | Walk down to the start, then read along the leaves |
| `WHERE price BETWEEN 10 AND 20` | Yes | The same, with an end point |
| `ORDER BY created_at LIMIT 10` | Yes | Read the first 10 leaf entries, already sorted |
| `WHERE name LIKE 'Sam%'` | Yes | A prefix is a range in sorted order |
| `WHERE name LIKE '%son'` | No | The matches are scattered through the order |

The last two rows are worth remembering. An index on text is sorted from the first character, so it helps with "starts with" and not with "ends with" or "contains". One PostgreSQL detail: for a prefix search the index must be sorted in plain character order, which is requested with `text_pattern_ops` when the database uses a language-specific ordering.

steps.title: When the database ignores an index
steps.text:
Having an index does not mean it is used. The database estimates the cost of each way of running a query and picks the cheapest.

An index lookup costs a few index pages plus one table page per matching row, and those table pages are scattered. For a handful of rows that is very cheap. For a large share of the table it is worse than a sequential scan, which reads every page once, in order.

The share of rows a condition keeps is called its **selectivity**. A condition that keeps few rows is selective, and an index on it helps. A condition that keeps most rows is not, and the index will be ignored.

- `WHERE id = 42` keeps one row in millions. The index is used.
- `WHERE status = 'active'` when 95% of rows are active keeps nearly everything. A sequential scan is cheaper, and the database is right to choose it.

steps.title: Low selectivity
steps.text: A `users` table has 10 million rows. The column `country` has 40 distinct values, and 60% of the users have `country = 'US'`. There is an index on `country`.

steps.title: Conditions that hide the column
steps.text:
An index on a column is sorted by that column's values. If the query wraps the column in a function or a calculation, the result is no longer something the index is sorted by, and the index cannot be used.

```sql
-- cannot use an index on created_at
SELECT * FROM orders WHERE date(created_at) = '2025-03-04';

-- can use it: the column is left bare, and the range is on the other side
SELECT * FROM orders
WHERE created_at >= '2025-03-04' AND created_at < '2025-03-05';
```

The same happens with `lower(email) = 'a@example.com'`, with `amount * 1.2 > 100`, and with converting the column to another type before comparing it, as in `account_id::text = '4411'`.

The rule is to keep the indexed column alone on one side of the comparison. When a function really is needed, PostgreSQL can index the expression itself:

```sql
CREATE INDEX users_lower_email_idx ON users (lower(email));
```

steps.title: What an index costs
steps.text:
Every index is paid for on every write.

- **Slower writes.** An `INSERT` adds an entry to every index on the table. An `UPDATE` of an indexed column changes its index. A table with eight indexes does nine writes for each row inserted.
- **Space.** An index can be a large fraction of the table's size. Several together can exceed it.
- **Memory.** Index pages compete with table pages for the buffer cache.

So an index is a trade: faster reads for one kind of question, in exchange for slower writes and more space. Add an index for a question the application asks often. Do not add one for every column in case it is useful.

Unused indexes are common in old systems. They cost writes for ever and help nothing. PostgreSQL counts how often each index is used, so they can be found and dropped.

steps.title: Unique indexes and primary keys
steps.text:
An index can also enforce a rule. A **unique index** refuses a second row with the same value.

```sql
CREATE UNIQUE INDEX users_email_key ON users (email);
```

A **primary key** is a unique, required column that identifies each row, and the database creates a unique index for it automatically. That is why looking a row up by its primary key is always fast, and why you never need to add an index on the primary key yourself.

A foreign key is different. In PostgreSQL, declaring that `orders.customer_id` refers to `customers.id` does not create an index on `orders.customer_id`. If you look up orders by customer, or delete customers, you need to add that index.

steps.title: Other kinds of index
steps.text:
A B-tree is the default and fits most columns. A few other kinds exist for data that a sorted order does not serve.

- A **hash index** answers only exact matches.
- A **GIN index** indexes the items inside a value: the words in a document, the keys in a JSON value, the elements of an array.
- A **GiST index** handles ranges and geometric data, such as "which areas contain this point".

You need to know that they exist. Reach for one when a B-tree cannot answer the question, such as searching for a word inside text.

steps.title: Which index helps
steps.text:
An application runs this query many times a second on a table of 50 million rows:

```sql
SELECT * FROM sessions WHERE lower(token) = 'ab12cd34';
```

There is a B-tree index on `token`.

steps.title: Exercise: choose the indexes
steps.text:
A `tickets` table for a support system has 30 million rows and these columns: `id` (primary key), `customer_id`, `status` (one of `open`, `pending`, `closed`, with 97% `closed`), `created_at`, `subject` and `body`.

The application runs these queries often:

1. Fetch one ticket by `id`.
2. List a customer's tickets.
3. List all `open` tickets, oldest first.
4. Find tickets whose `subject` contains a word.

For each, say whether an index exists already, which index you would add, or why a B-tree does not help. Then say which index you would not add, and why.

steps.title: One possible answer
steps.text:
1. **Already indexed.** The primary key has a unique index. Nothing to add.
2. **Add an index on `customer_id`.** One customer has a few tickets out of 30 million, so the condition is very selective.
3. **Add a partial index.** A plain index on `status` is poor: for `closed` it would never be used, and it stores 30 million entries to serve the 1% that are open. PostgreSQL can index only some of the rows:

```sql
CREATE INDEX tickets_open_idx ON tickets (created_at)
WHERE status = 'open';
```

It holds only the open tickets, sorted by date, so it is small and it returns them already in order.

4. **A B-tree does not help.** "Contains a word" is not a prefix, so the matches are not together in sorted order. This needs a full-text index, which is a GIN index over the words in the subject, or a separate search system.

**Not to add:** an index on `body`, and indexes on every column "to be safe". Each would slow down every insert and update of a ticket while serving no query on the list.

choices.text: With a sequential scan

choices.text: It cannot run it without an index on `country`

choices.text: No. The function hides the column, so every row is read
choices.feedback: The index knows nothing about the lowercased values. Index `lower(token)`, or store tokens in one case and compare without the function.

choices.text: Yes, but only for the first matching row
choices.feedback: An index is either usable for a condition or not. There is no partial use here.

lessons.title: Indexes on several columns
lessons.intro: Most real queries filter on more than one column and sort the result. One index on several columns can serve such a query completely, if its columns are in the right order. This module covers that order, and indexes that answer a query without touching the table.

steps.title: A composite index
steps.text:
A **composite index** (also called a multi-column index) is sorted by its first column, then by its second within equal values of the first, and so on. A phone book works the same way: sorted by surname, then by first name within each surname.

```sql
CREATE INDEX orders_customer_created_idx
  ON orders (customer_id, created_at);
```

In this index, all of one customer's orders sit next to each other, and within that group they are in date order.

steps.title: The leftmost prefix rule
steps.text:
A phone book finds "Okafor" at once, and "Okafor, Bilal" at once. It is useless for finding everyone called "Bilal", since they are scattered through every surname.

A composite index behaves the same way. It can be used for conditions on its first column, or its first two, or its first three. It cannot be used efficiently for a condition that skips the first column. This is the **leftmost prefix rule**.

For an index on `(customer_id, created_at)`:

| Condition | Index usable? |
| --- | --- |
| `customer_id = 17` | Yes |
| `customer_id = 17 AND created_at >= '2025-02-01'` | Yes, fully |
| `created_at >= '2025-02-01'` | No. The dates are scattered across all customers |

One practical result: an index on `(customer_id, created_at)` already serves every query that an index on `(customer_id)` alone would serve. Keeping both wastes a write on every insert.

steps.title: Choosing the column order
steps.text:
The order follows from how the query uses each column. A rule that works for most queries:

1. **Columns compared with `=` first.**
2. **Then the column used for a range or for sorting.**

The reason is how the index is read. Equality conditions narrow the search to one continuous stretch of the index. Inside that stretch, the next column is in sorted order, so a range on it is another continuous stretch, and an `ORDER BY` on it needs no sorting at all.

Once a range condition is applied to a column, the columns after it in the index are no longer in useful order, so they cannot narrow the search further.

steps.title: Which order
steps.text:
A query runs often:

```sql
SELECT * FROM messages
WHERE chat_id = 9001
ORDER BY sent_at DESC
LIMIT 50;
```

steps.title: Sorting for free
steps.text:
Sorting a large result is expensive. The database must collect every matching row and sort them, in memory if they fit and on disk if not, before it can return the first one.

An index is already sorted. When the `ORDER BY` matches the index order, the database reads the rows in that order and skips the sort. With a `LIMIT`, it stops as soon as it has enough rows.

This is the difference between a "latest 20 items" query that takes a millisecond and one that takes seconds. With the right index, it reads 20 entries. Without it, it finds all matching rows, sorts them and throws away all but 20.

steps.title: Covering indexes
steps.text:
An ordinary index lookup has two steps: find the entry in the index, then visit the table page for the rest of the row. The second step is the expensive one when there are many rows, since each visit is a separate page.

If the index contains every column the query needs, the second step can be skipped. This is an **index-only scan**, and the index is said to **cover** the query.

```sql
-- the query needs only these three columns
SELECT created_at, total FROM orders WHERE customer_id = 17;

-- an index that covers it
CREATE INDEX orders_customer_cover_idx
  ON orders (customer_id, created_at) INCLUDE (total);
```

`INCLUDE` adds columns to the leaf entries without making them part of the sort order. They are there only to be returned.

Covering has limits. Each added column makes the index larger and its upkeep costlier, and a query using `SELECT *` can never be covered. Use it for a small number of very frequent queries that return a few columns.

steps.title: Several single indexes are not the same
steps.text:
A table has an index on `status` and a separate index on `created_at`. A query filters on both. The database can use one of them and check the other condition row by row, or it can combine the two indexes, which PostgreSQL does with a **bitmap scan**: it collects the matching row locations from each index, intersects the two sets, and then visits the table.

That works, and it is slower than one composite index on both columns, which finds the exact stretch directly. If two columns are nearly always filtered together, give them one composite index.

steps.title: Too many indexes
steps.text:
It is tempting to add an index for every query. Each one slows every write. Review a table's indexes as a set.

- **Redundant.** `(a)` is redundant when `(a, b)` exists.
- **Duplicate.** Two indexes on the same columns in the same order, often created by different tools.
- **Unused.** Never chosen by any query.

A handful of well-chosen composite indexes usually serves a table better than a dozen single-column ones.

steps.title: Skipping the first column
steps.text:
A table has one index, on `(tenant_id, email)`. This query runs during login:

```sql
SELECT * FROM users WHERE email = 'ana@example.com';
```

steps.title: Exercise: design the indexes
steps.text:
An `invoices` table has 40 million rows with the columns `id`, `account_id`, `status` (`draft`, `sent`, `paid`, `overdue`), `due_date`, `amount` and `created_at`. These queries run often:

```sql
-- A: an account's invoices, newest first, one page at a time
SELECT * FROM invoices WHERE account_id = ?
ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT 25;

-- B: an account's overdue invoices
SELECT * FROM invoices WHERE account_id = ? AND status = 'overdue';

-- C: total owed per account, for a dashboard that refreshes often
SELECT sum(amount) FROM invoices
WHERE account_id = ? AND status IN ('sent', 'overdue');

-- D: everything due in the next 7 days, across all accounts
SELECT * FROM invoices
WHERE due_date BETWEEN ? AND ? AND status = 'sent';
```

Propose the smallest set of indexes that serves all four well. Explain the column order of each.

steps.title: One possible answer
steps.text:
**Index 1: `(account_id, created_at)`** serves A. Equality on `account_id` narrows to one account, and `created_at` gives the order, so the database reads 25 entries from the end and stops.

**Index 2: `(account_id, status) INCLUDE (amount)`** serves B and C. Both use equality on `account_id` and a condition on `status`. For C, the included `amount` makes it an index-only scan, so the dashboard never visits the table.

**Index 3: `(status, due_date)`** serves D. Equality on `status` first, then the range on `due_date`. With `(due_date, status)` the database would read every invoice due that week and discard the ones not `sent`. A partial index is a good alternative here: `(due_date) WHERE status = 'sent'`.

**Not added**

- `(account_id)` alone. Index 1 and index 2 both start with it.
- `(status)` alone. It has four values, and index 3 starts with it.
- An index on `amount` or `created_at` alone. No query needs one.

Three indexes for four queries is a reasonable outcome. If writes to this table were very heavy, index 2 could be dropped. Queries B and C would then use index 1 to find the account's invoices and filter them, which is acceptable while one account has only hundreds of invoices.

lessons.title: Read a query plan
lessons.intro: The database decides how to run each query, and it will show you its decision. This module covers how to ask for a plan, how to read one, and how to spot the difference between what the database expected and what happened.

steps.title: The planner
steps.text:
SQL says what you want, not how to get it. A part of the database called the **planner** (or optimizer) works out how. For one query there may be many ways: scan the table or use an index, join in one order or another. The planner estimates the cost of each and picks the cheapest.

The result is a **query plan**: a tree of steps. Each step takes rows from the steps below it and passes rows up.

To estimate costs, the planner needs to know roughly how many rows each step will produce. It gets that from **statistics** that the database keeps about every table: how many rows it has, how many distinct values each column has, which values are most common, and how values are spread.

steps.title: Ask for the plan
steps.text:
Put `EXPLAIN` in front of a query to see the plan without running it.

```sql
EXPLAIN SELECT * FROM orders WHERE customer_id = 17;
```

`EXPLAIN ANALYZE` runs the query and shows the plan together with what really happened: the true row counts and the time each step took.

```sql
EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) SELECT * FROM orders WHERE customer_id = 17;
```

`BUFFERS` adds the number of pages each step touched, which is the cost measure from the first module.

One warning. `EXPLAIN ANALYZE` really executes the statement. On an `UPDATE` or `DELETE` it changes the data. Wrap such a statement in a transaction and roll it back.

steps.title: Read one step
steps.text:
Each line of a plan is one step with the same parts.


Three things deserve attention first.

- The **type of step**: how the rows were found.
- **Estimated rows against actual rows**: whether the planner's picture of the data was right.
- **Where the time is**: which step accounts for most of it.

The cost numbers have no unit you can convert to milliseconds. They are for comparing one plan with another.

steps.title: The common steps
steps.text:
| Step | What it does | Good when |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Seq Scan | Reads every page of the table | The query needs a large share of the rows |
| Index Scan | Finds entries in an index, then visits the table for each | Few rows match |
| Index Only Scan | Answers from the index alone | The index covers the query |
| Bitmap Heap Scan | Collects row locations from an index, sorts them by page, then visits each page once | A middling number of rows match |
| Sort | Sorts its input | No index gives the order |
| Hash Join, Nested Loop, Merge Join | Three ways to join, covered in the next module | |
| Aggregate | Computes `count`, `sum`, `GROUP BY` | |
| Limit | Stops after N rows | |

A `Seq Scan` is not a fault in itself. On a small table, or for a query that needs most of the rows, it is the right choice. It is a fault when it reads millions of rows to return a few.

steps.title: Read a tree
steps.text:
A plan with several steps is indented. Each step's inputs are the more deeply indented steps beneath it. Read it from the innermost steps outward: those run first and feed the steps above.


This plan works, and it shows something to improve. The database fetched and sorted 180 rows to return 20. An index on `(customer_id, created_at)` would return them in order, and the `Sort` step would disappear.

steps.title: Rows removed by a filter
steps.text:
A line that reads `Rows Removed by Filter` tells you how much work was wasted. The step read those rows and threw them away.


This is the clearest sign that an index is missing. The ratio of rows removed to rows kept is the size of the waste.

The difference between `Index Cond` and `Filter` under an index scan carries the same meaning. A condition listed as `Index Cond` was used to find the entries. A condition listed as `Filter` was checked afterwards, row by row.

steps.title: What the plan says
steps.text:
A query for one user's notifications shows this step:

```text
Seq Scan on notifications  (actual time=0.03..1210.50 rows=12 loops=1)
  Filter: (user_id = 5521)
  Rows Removed by Filter: 31999988
```

steps.title: When the estimate is wrong
steps.text:
The planner chooses a plan from its row estimates. When an estimate is far off, it can choose badly. In `EXPLAIN ANALYZE`, compare `rows=` in the estimate with `rows=` in the actual part, for each step.

A step that expected 10 rows and produced 800,000 is the place to look. The planner chose a method that suits 10 rows, and it was run on 800,000.

Common causes of bad estimates:

- **Stale statistics.** The table changed a lot since statistics were last gathered. Running `ANALYZE tablename` refreshes them. PostgreSQL does this automatically in the background, and a large load of data can get ahead of it.
- **Related columns.** The planner assumes columns are independent. If `city = 'Paris'` and `country = 'France'` are both in the query, it multiplies the two shares and expects far fewer rows than exist.
- **Conditions it cannot see into**, such as a function applied to a column.

steps.title: The same query, two plans
steps.text:
A query can be fast for one value and slow for another. Looking up the orders of a normal customer returns 10 rows, and an index scan is ideal. Looking up the orders of the one enormous customer returns a third of the table, and a different plan would be better.

Data that is unevenly spread like this is called **skewed**. It explains reports such as "the page is slow only for this one account". When you investigate, use `EXPLAIN ANALYZE` with the exact values from the slow case.

steps.title: Loops multiply
steps.text:
`loops` is how many times a step ran. The time and rows shown for a step are for one loop. A step with `actual time=0.05 rows=1 loops=40000` did not take 0.05 ms. It took 0.05 ms forty thousand times, which is 2 seconds.

Missing this is the most common mistake in reading a plan. Always multiply by `loops` before deciding which step is slow.

steps.title: Which step is slow
steps.text:
A plan contains these two steps:

```text
->  Seq Scan on customers   (actual time=0.01..35.00 rows=50000 loops=1)
->  Index Scan on orders    (actual time=0.02..0.06 rows=4 loops=50000)
```

steps.title: Exercise: read a plan
steps.text:
A dashboard query takes 4 seconds. Here is its plan.


Answer these: which step takes the time, how many rows it read and kept, whether the estimate was right, and what you would do. Say whether the `Sort` at the top is a problem.

steps.title: One possible answer
steps.text:
**Where the time goes.** The `Seq Scan` finishes at 3,650 ms out of 4,102. The aggregate and the sort add under half a second together.

**Rows.** It read about 60 million rows, kept 2.1 million and threw away 58 million. It read 750,000 pages, all from disk (`read`, not `hit`).

**The estimate.** It expected 900 rows and got 2.1 million. The statistics are badly out of date, probably because a lot of recent data was loaded since they were gathered. Here the plan would be a sequential scan either way, since no index exists. A wrong estimate like this can still mislead the steps above it, so run `ANALYZE signups`.

**The fix.** Add an index on `created_at`. The condition keeps 2.1 million of 60 million rows, about 3.5%, which is selective enough for an index to pay off. Since the query needs only `country` from each row, an index on `(created_at) INCLUDE (country)` allows an index-only scan and avoids the table completely.

**The sort.** It sorts 40 rows, one per country, in a fraction of a millisecond. It is not a problem. A `Sort` matters when its input is large.

For a dashboard that refreshes often, a further step is to keep a small table of daily counts per country and query that. That idea is covered in the module on duplicating data.

lessons.title: How joins are run
lessons.intro: A join combines rows from two tables. The database has three ways to do it, and each suits a different amount of data. This module covers the three methods, how to recognise them in a plan, and the join mistakes that make queries slow.

steps.title: The problem a join solves
steps.text:
A join asks: for each row in one table, which rows in the other table match it? With 10,000 customers and 1 million orders, comparing every pair would mean 10 billion comparisons. The three join methods are three ways of avoiding that.

Which one the planner picks depends on how many rows come from each side and on which indexes exist. So a join can be fast with one set of values and slow with another, although the SQL is the same.

```sql
SELECT c.name, o.total
FROM customers c
JOIN orders o ON o.customer_id = c.id
WHERE c.country = 'NZ';
```

steps.title: Nested loop
steps.text:
A **nested loop** takes each row from the first table (the outer side) and looks up its matches in the second table (the inner side).

If the inner side has an index on the join column, each lookup is a quick index scan. The total cost is the number of outer rows multiplied by the cost of one lookup.

That makes a nested loop the best method when the outer side is small: a few rows or a few hundred. It is also the only method that can return its first rows at once, which matters for queries with a small `LIMIT`.

It becomes very slow when the outer side is large, because the lookup is repeated for every row. And without an index on the inner side, each "lookup" is a scan of the whole inner table.

steps.title: Hash join
steps.text:
A **hash join** reads the smaller table once and builds a lookup table from it in memory, keyed by the join column. This lookup table is a hash table. It then reads the larger table once and, for each row, checks the hash table for a match.

Each table is read exactly once, and each check is a single memory operation. No index is needed. That makes a hash join the usual choice when both sides are large and most of their rows take part.

Its costs are memory and a slow start. The hash table must fit in the memory allowed for one operation. If it does not, the database splits the work into batches written to temporary files on disk, which is much slower. And no row can be returned until the hash table is complete.

A hash join works only for equality conditions (`a.x = b.x`).

steps.title: Merge join
steps.text:
A **merge join** needs both inputs sorted by the join column. It then walks down both at the same time, like closing a zip, and matches rows as it goes.

If both sides are already sorted, because an index provides that order, a merge join is very cheap and needs almost no memory. If they are not, the database has to sort them first, and the sort is the expensive part.

It is the method for joining two very large inputs that are already in order.

| Method | Best when | Needs | Weak when |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Nested loop | One side is small | An index on the inner side | The outer side is large |
| Hash join | Both sides are large | Memory for the smaller side | The smaller side does not fit in memory |
| Merge join | Both sides are already sorted | Sorted inputs | The inputs must be sorted first |

steps.title: The wrong method
steps.text: A plan shows a nested loop. The planner expected 5 rows from the outer side. In `EXPLAIN ANALYZE` the outer side produced 400,000 rows, and the inner index scan shows `loops=400000`.

steps.title: Index the join columns
steps.text:
For a nested loop to be cheap, the inner side needs an index on the column being matched. Primary keys always have one. Foreign key columns do not get one automatically in PostgreSQL.

So this is one of the most common causes of a slow join: a query finds a few customers and then needs their orders, and `orders.customer_id` has no index. Each "lookup" scans the whole `orders` table.

The rule of thumb is to index every foreign key column that you join on or filter by. It also speeds up deleting a parent row, since the database must check for children.

steps.title: Filter before joining
steps.text:
The fewer rows that enter a join, the cheaper it is. The planner tries to apply conditions as early as it can, and it also chooses the order in which tables are joined, starting with whatever produces the fewest rows.

You help it most by giving it conditions it can use.

- Put selective conditions on indexed columns.
- Keep statistics current, so the planner knows which side is small.
- Avoid wrapping join columns in functions or joining columns of different types. Both stop an index from being used.

With many tables, the number of possible join orders grows very quickly, and the planner cannot try them all. Queries that join eight or ten tables are the ones where plans most often go wrong.

steps.title: Joins that multiply rows
steps.text:
A join returns one row for every matching pair. When one row on the left matches several on the right, the left row is repeated. Joining to two such tables at once multiplies them together.

```sql
SELECT c.id, sum(o.total), count(t.id)
FROM customers c
JOIN orders o  ON o.customer_id = c.id
JOIN tickets t ON t.customer_id = c.id
GROUP BY c.id;
```

A customer with 10 orders and 5 tickets produces 50 rows before grouping. Each order is counted 5 times, so the sum is 5 times too large, and the ticket count is 10 times too large. The query runs without error and returns wrong numbers.

The fix is to total each table separately, in a subquery, and then join the totals, so that each side has one row per customer.

steps.title: One query per row
steps.text:
A join problem often lives in the application, not in SQL. Code fetches a list of 100 orders with one query, then loops over them and runs one more query per order to fetch its customer. That is 101 queries where one join would do.

It is called the **N+1 problem**. Each query is fast, so nothing looks slow in the database's own statistics. The time goes into 100 extra round trips. It appears most with libraries that load related data automatically when a property is first read.

The cure is to fetch the related rows together: a join, or one second query with `WHERE customer_id IN (...)` for the whole list.

steps.title: Wrong totals
steps.text: A report joins `products` to `order_lines` and to `reviews`, and computes `sum(order_lines.quantity)` per product. A product has 200 order lines and 12 reviews.

steps.title: Exercise: diagnose the join
steps.text:
An "account overview" page is slow for large accounts and fine for small ones. Its query joins `accounts`, `users`, `projects` and `tasks` to list every task for an account. You are given these facts.

1. The plan uses nested loops throughout.
2. For a small account, the `projects` step returns 3 rows. For the slow account it returns 40,000, and the planner estimated 5.
3. The step on `tasks` is a `Seq Scan` with `Filter: (project_id = ...)` and `loops=40000`.
4. `tasks.project_id` is a foreign key with no index.

Explain why the page is slow for large accounts only. List the changes you would make, with the most important first.

steps.title: One possible answer
steps.text:
**Why only large accounts.** For a small account, the nested loop runs the inner step 3 times. For the large one it runs it 40,000 times. And that inner step is a sequential scan of the entire `tasks` table, since `project_id` has no index. Forty thousand full scans of a large table is the whole problem. For 3 projects, the same flaw is 3 scans and goes unnoticed.

**Changes, in order**

1. **Add an index on `tasks.project_id`.** Each inner lookup becomes an index scan of a few pages. This alone turns the query from unusable to acceptable. It also fixes the same hidden cost for every other query that finds tasks by project.
2. **Refresh the statistics** with `ANALYZE` on `projects`, and find out why the estimate is 5 when the truth is 40,000. This account is an outlier in skewed data. With a correct estimate, the planner would choose a hash join for the large account: read the account's projects once and read the tasks once.
3. **Check the other foreign keys** in the query (`users.account_id`, `projects.account_id`) for the same missing index.
4. **Look at the page itself.** Listing every task of 40,000 projects on one page is rarely what anyone needs. Paging the result, or showing counts with the detail on request, removes most of the work.

The first change is the fix. The fourth is the one that questions whether the query should exist in this form.

lessons.title: Model the data
lessons.intro: The shape of the tables decides which mistakes the database can prevent and which queries are easy. This module covers keys, relationships, the rule of storing each fact once, and the constraints that keep bad data out.

steps.title: Each table is one kind of thing
steps.text:
A good table describes one kind of thing, and each row is one of them: one customer, one order, one product. Each column is one fact about that thing.

A quick test for a design is to say what a row means in one sentence. "Each row is one order" is clear. "Each row is an order, or sometimes a refund, and the last three columns apply only to subscriptions" describes a table that is doing several jobs.

steps.title: Keys
steps.text:
Every table needs a **primary key**: a column, or a set of columns, whose value identifies exactly one row and never changes.

There are two kinds.

- A **natural key** is a value from the real world: an email address, a tax number, a product code.
- A **surrogate key** is a value made up for the purpose, with no meaning: a number from a sequence, or a UUID (a long random identifier).

Natural keys look attractive and cause trouble, because real-world values change. People change email addresses. Product codes are reissued. When a key changes, every row in every other table that refers to it has to change too.

The usual advice is a surrogate primary key, plus a unique constraint on the natural value. The row keeps a stable identity, and duplicates are still refused.

```sql
CREATE TABLE customers (
  id     bigint GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY,
  email  text NOT NULL UNIQUE,
  name   text NOT NULL
);
```

steps.title: Relationships
steps.text:
Tables refer to each other with a **foreign key**: a column that holds the primary key of a row in another table.

There are three shapes of relationship.

- **One to many.** One customer has many orders. The "many" side holds the foreign key: `orders.customer_id`.
- **Many to many.** A student takes many courses, and a course has many students. Neither table can hold the key. A third table, with one row per pair, connects them.
- **One to one.** A user has one profile. It is rare. It is used to split off columns that are optional, large or need different access.

steps.title: Store each fact once
steps.text:
The central rule of relational design is that each fact is stored in exactly one place. A design that follows it is called **normalized**.

Look at an `orders` table that also stores the customer's name and email in every row. The customer's email is now recorded once per order. Three problems follow.

- **Update.** When the email changes, every order row has to be changed. If one is missed, the database holds two different emails for one customer.
- **Insert.** A customer with no orders cannot be recorded at all.
- **Delete.** Deleting a customer's only order also deletes the only record of their email.

The fix is to move the customer's facts to a `customers` table and leave only `customer_id` in `orders`. The email is stored once, and a change is one update.

steps.title: A practical test
steps.text:
The formal rules of normalization are called normal forms. In practice, three questions catch nearly every problem.

1. **Is any column a list?** A column `tags` that holds `"red,large,sale"` cannot be indexed, searched or constrained properly. Lists belong in their own table, one row per item.
2. **Are there numbered columns?** `phone1`, `phone2`, `phone3` is a list in disguise. What happens with a fourth phone?
3. **Does any column describe something other than this row's thing?** In an `orders` table, `customer_email` describes the customer, not the order. It belongs with the customer.

steps.title: Not everything that repeats is a duplicate
steps.text:
One case looks like a violation and is not. An order line stores the price that was charged, although the product also has a price.

These are two different facts. `products.price` is what the product costs now. `order_lines.unit_price` is what this customer paid on that day. If the order line only pointed at the product, last year's invoices would change whenever a price was updated.

Ask whether the value should change when the source changes. If yes, store it once and join. If it must be frozen at a moment in time, copy it, and name the column to make that clear.

steps.title: Frozen or live
steps.text: An invoicing system stores a customer's billing address in the `customers` table only. An invoice row holds `customer_id` and the amounts. A customer moves and updates their address.

steps.title: Constraints
steps.text:
A **constraint** is a rule that the database enforces on every write, whichever application or script does the writing.

| Constraint | Guarantees |
| --- | --- |
| `NOT NULL` | The column always has a value |
| `UNIQUE` | No two rows share the value |
| `PRIMARY KEY` | Unique, required, and identifies the row |
| `FOREIGN KEY` | The value refers to a row that exists |
| `CHECK` | A condition holds, such as `quantity > 0` |

Checks in application code are useful, and they are not enough. Bugs skip them, a second application does not have them, and a manual fix at 03:00 does not go through them. A constraint in the database holds whatever happens above it.

Constraints are also documentation that cannot go out of date. A `NOT NULL` column tells every reader of the schema that the value is always there.

```sql
CREATE TABLE order_lines (
  order_id    bigint  NOT NULL REFERENCES orders (id),
  product_id  bigint  NOT NULL REFERENCES products (id),
  quantity    integer NOT NULL CHECK (quantity > 0),
  unit_price  numeric(10, 2) NOT NULL CHECK (unit_price >= 0),
  PRIMARY KEY (order_id, product_id)
);
```

steps.title: Choose types that fit
steps.text:
A column's type is its first constraint.

- **Money** goes in an exact decimal type, never a floating-point one. Floating point cannot represent 0.10 exactly, and totals drift.
- **A moment in time** goes in a timestamp with time zone, stored in UTC. A timestamp without a zone is ambiguous as soon as two servers or two countries are involved.
- **Yes or no** goes in a boolean, not in text holding `'Y'` or `'yes'` or `'1'`.
- **One of a fixed set** goes in a column with a `CHECK`, an enum type, or a foreign key to a small lookup table.
- **Dates and numbers** never go in text columns. As text, `'10'` sorts before `'9'`.

steps.title: NULL means unknown
steps.text:
`NULL` marks a missing value. It does not behave like an ordinary value, which surprises people.

- Any comparison with `NULL` gives unknown, not true or false. `WHERE discount <> 10` does not return rows where `discount` is `NULL`.
- `NULL = NULL` is not true. Test with `IS NULL`.
- `count(column)` skips `NULL` values. `count(*)` does not.

Decide for each column whether a missing value can really occur. If it cannot, declare `NOT NULL`. Every nullable column is a case that each query has to think about.

steps.title: The missing rows
steps.text:
A `tasks` table has a nullable `assignee_id`. A report runs:

```sql
SELECT count(*) FROM tasks WHERE assignee_id <> 42;
```

The table has 100 tasks: 30 assigned to user 42, 50 assigned to others, and 20 unassigned.

steps.title: Exercise: fix the schema
steps.text:
A small library keeps everything in one table.


List the problems. Then design tables that fix them, with keys, types and constraints. Note that the library owns several copies of some books.

steps.title: One possible answer
steps.text:
**Problems**

- A member's name and phones are repeated per loan, and the two rows for Ana already disagree about her phones.
- `member_phones` is a list in one column.
- Book title and author are repeated per loan.
- A member with no loans, or a book never borrowed, cannot be recorded.
- `due_date` is text in two formats. `returned` is text with three spellings of two values.
- Nothing says which copy of "Dune" was lent.

**Tables**

```sql
CREATE TABLE members (
  id    bigint GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY,
  name  text NOT NULL
);

CREATE TABLE member_phones (
  member_id  bigint NOT NULL REFERENCES members (id),
  phone      text   NOT NULL,
  PRIMARY KEY (member_id, phone)
);

CREATE TABLE books (
  id      bigint GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY,
  title   text NOT NULL,
  author  text NOT NULL
);

CREATE TABLE copies (
  id       bigint GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY,
  book_id  bigint NOT NULL REFERENCES books (id)
);

CREATE TABLE loans (
  id           bigint GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY,
  copy_id      bigint NOT NULL REFERENCES copies (id),
  member_id    bigint NOT NULL REFERENCES members (id),
  due_date     date   NOT NULL,
  returned_at  timestamptz
);
```

`returned_at` replaces the yes/no column. An empty value means the copy is still out, and a value says when it came back, which is more useful than a flag. This is a case where `NULL` has one clear meaning.

One more rule is worth enforcing: a copy can be out on only one loan at a time. A partial unique index does it, on `loans (copy_id) WHERE returned_at IS NULL`.

Indexes on `loans.member_id` and `copies.book_id` are needed as well, since foreign keys do not create them.

lessons.title: When to duplicate data
lessons.intro: Storing each fact once keeps data correct. Sometimes it also makes a frequent read too slow. This module covers when to store a second copy on purpose, the ways to keep it right, and where flexible columns such as JSON fit.

steps.title: The cost of the clean design
steps.text:
A normalized design answers every question by joining and totalling at the moment it is asked. Usually that is fast enough. Sometimes it is not.

Take a forum page that lists 50 threads with the number of replies in each. In a normalized design the count comes from the `replies` table, computed for 50 threads on every page view. With millions of replies and a busy page, that is real work repeated thousands of times a minute, to show numbers that seldom change.

**Denormalization** means storing a copy of data, or a value computed from it, so that a read does not have to work it out. A `reply_count` column on the `threads` table is the standard example.

It is a trade. Reads become cheaper. Writes become more expensive, and there are now two places that can disagree.

steps.title: Normalize first
steps.text:
Denormalize only after the normalized design has been tried and measured. In order:

1. Is there a missing index? Most "slow joins" are this.
2. Is the query asking for more than it needs?
3. Would a cache in front of the query do?
4. Only then, store a derived value.

The reason for the order is that the first three can be undone at no cost. A duplicated value has to be kept correct for as long as the system lives, by every piece of code that writes to the source.

steps.title: Three kinds of duplication
steps.text:
| Kind | Example | Purpose |
| --- | --- | --- |
| A stored total | `threads.reply_count` | Avoid counting on every read |
| A copied column | `orders.customer_name` beside `customer_id` | Avoid a join on a hot path |
| A summary table | `daily_sales (day, product_id, units, revenue)` | Avoid scanning millions of rows for a report |

The third is the most useful and the least risky. A summary table is separate from the source data, it is clearly derived, and it can be thrown away and rebuilt at any time.

steps.title: Keeping the copy right
steps.text:
A duplicated value is only as good as the mechanism that updates it. There are four, from strictest to loosest.

**In the same transaction.** The code that inserts a reply also runs `UPDATE threads SET reply_count = reply_count + 1`, in one transaction. The count is always exact. Every code path that adds or removes a reply must remember to do it.

**A trigger.** The database runs the update itself whenever a row is inserted or deleted in `replies`. No code path can forget. The logic is now hidden in the database, where people do not expect it, and it adds work to every write.

**A materialized view.** The database stores the result of a query as a table. You refresh it on a schedule. Between refreshes it is out of date.

**A background job.** A scheduled task recomputes the values every few minutes or hours. It is simple, it corrects itself, and it is the least fresh.

| Method | Freshness | Risk |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Same transaction | Exact | A code path forgets |
| Trigger | Exact | Hidden logic, slower writes |
| Materialized view | As of the last refresh | Stale between refreshes |
| Background job | Minutes to hours old | Stale, and the simplest to get right |

steps.title: The counter that drifted
steps.text: A `threads.reply_count` column is increased by the application whenever a reply is posted. Months later, a moderation tool is added that deletes spam replies directly from the `replies` table. It does not touch `threads`.

steps.title: Plan for drift
steps.text:
Assume that any duplicated value will be wrong sooner or later: a bug, a manual fix, a failed job, a new tool. Build the repair in from the start.

- **Keep the source of truth.** The `replies` rows are the truth. The count is a convenience. Never keep only the derived value.
- **Be able to rebuild.** Have a query or job that recomputes every derived value from the source. Run it on a schedule, so errors correct themselves.
- **Check.** Compare a sample of stored values with freshly computed ones and alert on a difference.

A derived value that can be rebuilt is a safe optimisation. One that cannot be rebuilt has quietly become the only copy of some facts, with no way to tell whether it is right.

steps.title: A hot counter
steps.text:
Stored counters have a second problem under heavy writing. Every reply to a popular thread updates the same row in `threads`. Updates to one row happen one at a time, so the writers queue up behind each other. A post that gets thousands of likes a second turns its counter row into a bottleneck.

Two designs avoid it.

- **Count in the background.** Insert the like rows without touching a counter, and let a job update the total every few seconds. The count is slightly behind, which is usually acceptable.
- **Split the counter.** Keep several counter rows per post, add to one chosen at random, and sum them when reading.

steps.title: JSON columns
steps.text:
PostgreSQL can store a JSON document in a column (the `jsonb` type) and query inside it. This relaxes the fixed table structure for part of a row.

It suits data whose shape really varies or is not yours to define.

- Settings that differ for each kind of integration.
- The raw payload received from an external system.
- Optional attributes that differ per product category.

It suits badly anything you filter by, join on or need to trust. Inside a JSON value there are no column types, no `NOT NULL`, no foreign keys. A misspelt key is accepted without complaint. Queries into JSON are slower and need special indexes.

A good rule is that columns you query by, and columns that must be correct, are real columns. The loosely shaped remainder can be JSON. If a JSON field starts to appear in `WHERE` clauses, promote it to a real column.

steps.title: History and audit data
steps.text:
Another reason to store more than the current state is to know what happened. An `orders.status` column tells you the status now. It cannot tell you when the order was paid or who cancelled it.

The usual design is an append-only table of events beside the current-state table: `order_events (order_id, happened_at, kind, actor, details)`. Rows are only ever inserted. The current state can be rebuilt from them, and questions about the past have answers.

This is also duplication, with a clear owner. The event rows are the record, and the status column is a summary of them.

steps.title: Which mechanism
steps.text: A finance dashboard shows revenue per product per month for the last three years. It is opened a few dozen times a day. The source is 400 million order lines, and the query takes 90 seconds. Figures from yesterday are acceptable.

steps.title: Exercise: decide what to duplicate
steps.text:
A recipe site has `recipes` (200,000 rows), `ratings` (60 million rows, one per user per recipe) and `users`. Three pages are slow.

1. The recipe page shows the average rating and the number of ratings. It gets 800 views a second.
2. The home page lists the 20 highest-rated recipes of the past week.
3. Each rating on a recipe page shows the reviewer's display name, fetched by joining `users`.

For each, say whether you would denormalize, what you would store and how it is kept correct. Say which of the three you would leave normalized.

steps.title: One possible answer
steps.text:
1. **Denormalize.** Store `rating_count` and `rating_sum` on `recipes`, and compute the average as their ratio when reading. Two numbers that can be added to are easier to keep right than a stored average. Update them in the same transaction as each rating. One caution: when a user changes an earlier rating, adjust the sum by the difference. A nightly job recomputes both columns from `ratings` to repair any drift. At 800 views a second this removes 800 aggregate queries a second.

2. **A summary, refreshed on a schedule.** "Top 20 of the past week" need not be exact to the second. A job computes the list every 10 minutes into a small table or a cache entry. The home page reads 20 rows.

3. **Leave it normalized.** A page shows perhaps 20 ratings, and fetching 20 users by primary key is a few milliseconds. Copying the display name onto 60 million rating rows would mean updating all of a user's ratings whenever they rename themselves. The join is cheap and the copy is expensive. If this page is slow, the cause is elsewhere. Look for a missing index on `ratings.recipe_id`, or a query per rating.

The third case is the common trap: denormalizing a join that was never the problem. Measure first.

lessons.title: Transactions
lessons.intro: A transaction groups several changes into one unit that either happens completely or does not happen. This module covers what a transaction guarantees, how to use one, and the habits that make transactions cause trouble.

steps.title: The problem
Four guarantees
steps.text:
The guarantees are summarised as **ACID**.

| Letter | Name | Meaning |
| --- | --- | --- |
| A | Atomicity | All of the changes happen, or none do |
| C | Consistency | Every constraint holds when the transaction ends |
| I | Isolation | Transactions running at the same time do not see each other's unfinished work |
| D | Durability | Once committed, a change survives a crash |

Atomicity and durability come from the write-ahead log described in the first module. Each change is logged before it is applied, and a commit is confirmed only when its log record is safely on disk. After a crash, the database replays the log, keeps what was committed and undoes what was not.

Isolation has several strengths, and it is the subject of the next module.

steps.title: Every statement is in a transaction
steps.text:
In PostgreSQL, a single statement run by itself is wrapped in its own transaction and committed at once. This is called **autocommit**.

So one `UPDATE` that changes a million rows is atomic too. If it fails on row 900,000, none of the million rows are changed.

You need an explicit `BEGIN` only when several statements must succeed or fail together.

steps.title: Errors inside a transaction
steps.text:
When a statement fails inside a PostgreSQL transaction, the transaction is marked as failed. Every later statement is refused until you issue `ROLLBACK`.

This is deliberate. It stops a program from continuing with half of its work done. The correct reaction to an error in a transaction is to roll back and, if it makes sense, try the whole transaction again from the start.

A **savepoint** marks a place inside a transaction to which you can roll back without discarding everything before it. It is used when one optional step may fail.

```sql
BEGIN;
INSERT INTO orders (...) VALUES (...);
SAVEPOINT before_coupon;
UPDATE coupons SET used = true WHERE code = 'SPRING';  -- may fail
ROLLBACK TO before_coupon;   -- if it failed: undo only that step
COMMIT;                      -- the order is still saved
```

steps.title: Crash after commit
steps.text: An application runs `COMMIT` and receives the confirmation. One second later the database server loses power, before the changed pages were written to the table files.

steps.title: Keep transactions short
steps.text:
A transaction that is open holds things that other work needs.

- **Locks.** Rows it has changed are locked until it ends. Others who want to change them wait.
- **Old row versions.** While a transaction is open, the database cannot clean up row versions that the transaction might still need to see. A transaction left open for hours makes tables bloat.
- **A connection.** It occupies one for its whole duration.

So a transaction should contain only database work, and be finished as quickly as possible. The classic mistake is doing something slow in the middle.


Never wait for a person, a network call or a slow computation while a transaction is open.

steps.title: Idle in transaction
steps.text:
A connection that has run `BEGIN`, done some work and then gone silent is **idle in transaction**. The application may have crashed, hit an exception path that skipped the rollback, or simply be waiting for something.

It is one of the most damaging states a database can be in. The transaction still holds its locks and still blocks cleanup, and it does nothing useful. Other queries pile up behind it.

Two protections are worth having.

- In code, always end a transaction in a `finally` block or with the language's equivalent construct, so that every path commits or rolls back.
- In the database, set a time limit after which an idle transaction is ended automatically. In PostgreSQL this is `idle_in_transaction_session_timeout`.

steps.title: What a transaction does not cover
steps.text:
A transaction covers changes in one database. It does not cover anything outside it.

- An email that was sent cannot be unsent by `ROLLBACK`.
- A call to a payment provider is not undone.
- A message published to a queue has left.
- A file written to disk stays written.

When one action must change the database and do something external, order the work with care. Do the external step so that it can be repeated safely, or record the intent in the database inside the transaction and let a separate process carry it out afterwards. That second approach is the outbox pattern, which the system design course covers.

steps.title: The email that went out
steps.text: A sign-up handler does this inside one transaction: insert the user, send a welcome email, insert a default workspace. The third step fails with an error, and the transaction is rolled back.

steps.title: Batches
steps.text:
A very large change in one transaction has costs of its own. Deleting 50 million old rows in one statement holds locks for the whole run, produces a huge amount of log, delays replicas, and loses everything if it fails near the end.

Do such work in **batches**: a few thousand rows per transaction, in a loop, with a short pause between them. Each batch commits quickly. The job can be stopped and resumed, and other work is not blocked for long.

```sql
-- repeat until it deletes no rows
DELETE FROM events
WHERE id IN (
  SELECT id FROM events
  WHERE created_at < '2023-01-01'
  LIMIT 5000
);
```

The trade is atomicity. Halfway through, half of the rows are gone. That is fine for a cleanup. It is wrong for a change that must appear all at once.

steps.title: Exercise: find the faults
steps.text:
A "checkout" function does the following, in one transaction, in this order.

1. `BEGIN`
2. Insert the order row.
3. Call the payment provider's API and wait for the answer, which takes 1 to 8 seconds.
4. If the payment fails, return an error to the caller.
5. Decrease the stock of each product.
6. Send a confirmation email.
7. `COMMIT`

List what is wrong, with the consequence of each. Then rewrite the sequence.

steps.title: One possible answer
steps.text:
**Faults**

- **A network call inside the transaction (step 3).** The transaction is open for up to 8 seconds, and under load there are many of them. Each holds a connection the whole time, so the pool runs dry.
- **A path with no rollback (step 4).** The function returns without ending the transaction. The connection goes back to the pool idle in transaction, still holding the order row and blocking cleanup.
- **Payment taken, then a possible failure (step 5).** If decreasing stock fails, the transaction rolls back and the order disappears. The customer's card was charged, and no record of the order remains.
- **Email before commit (step 6).** If the commit fails, the customer has a confirmation for an order that does not exist.

**Rewritten**

1. In a short transaction: insert the order with the status `pending` and reserve the stock. Commit.
2. Outside any transaction: call the payment provider, with the order ID as the idempotency key.
3. In a second short transaction: on success, set the order to `paid`. On failure, set it to `failed` and release the stock. Commit.
4. After that commit: queue the confirmation email.

Each transaction now lasts milliseconds and contains only database work. The order row exists before the charge, so a crash at any point leaves a `pending` order that a background job can finish or cancel. Every path ends its transaction.

lessons.title: Isolation levels
lessons.intro: Many transactions run at the same time, and they read and change the same rows. Isolation decides how much they see of each other. This module covers what can go wrong, the levels that prevent it, and how to choose one.

steps.title: Why isolation is a choice
steps.text:
The simplest way to keep transactions from interfering would be to run them one at a time. The result would always be correct, and the database would be very slow.

So databases run transactions side by side and offer several **isolation levels**. A stricter level prevents more kinds of interference and costs more: more waiting, or more transactions that fail and must be tried again. A looser level is faster and allows specific odd results, called **anomalies**.

To choose a level, you need to know the anomalies.

steps.title: Row versions and snapshots
steps.text:
PostgreSQL keeps old versions of rows, as the first module described. It uses them to give each query or transaction a **snapshot**: a consistent view of the data as it was at one moment.

A reader looks at the versions that were committed when its snapshot was taken, and ignores newer ones. This design is called **MVCC** (multi-version concurrency control). Its main benefit is that readers never block writers and writers never block readers. A long report does not stop orders from being placed.

What differs between isolation levels is when the snapshot is taken.

steps.title: The anomalies
steps.text:
| Anomaly | What happens |
| --- | --- |
| Dirty read | You read a change that another transaction has not committed, and it is then rolled back |
| Non-repeatable read | You read a row twice in one transaction and get different values, because someone committed a change in between |
| Phantom read | You run the same search twice and get different rows, because someone inserted or deleted matching rows |
| Lost update | Two transactions read a value, both change it and write it back, and one change overwrites the other |
| Write skew | Two transactions each check a rule, each make a change that is fine alone, and together they break the rule |

The last two are the ones that cause real bugs in applications. They do not look like errors. Each transaction succeeds, and the data ends up wrong.

steps.title: Lost update
steps.text:
Two people buy the last items of a product at the same moment. The application reads the stock, subtracts in code and writes the result back.


Both transactions did what they were written to do. The fault is the pattern "read, compute in the application, write back", which leaves a gap between the read and the write.

steps.title: The levels
steps.text:
The SQL standard defines four levels. PostgreSQL implements three distinct behaviours, since its Read Uncommitted behaves as Read Committed.

| Level | Snapshot taken | Prevents | Still allows |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Read Committed (the default) | At the start of each statement | Dirty reads | Non-repeatable reads, phantoms, lost updates in read-then-write code, write skew |
| Repeatable Read | At the start of the transaction | The above, plus non-repeatable reads and phantoms. A lost update is detected and one transaction fails | Write skew |
| Serializable | At the start of the transaction, with extra checking | Everything. The result equals some one-at-a-time order | Nothing, and transactions may fail and need a retry |

Other databases differ in the details and in their defaults. Check the documentation of the one you use before relying on a level's name.

steps.title: Read Committed in practice
steps.text:
Read Committed is the default, and most applications run on it without knowing. Each statement sees everything committed before that statement began.

Two consequences are worth knowing.

- Two statements in the same transaction can see different data. A report that runs a count and then a sum may get results that do not agree with each other.
- "Read, then decide, then write" is unsafe, as the lost update showed. The value may have changed after it was read.

For a transaction of several statements that must agree with each other, such as a multi-part report, Repeatable Read gives one consistent snapshot for all of them.

steps.title: The report that did not add up
steps.text: A transaction at Read Committed runs two statements a moment apart: first `SELECT count(*) FROM orders WHERE day = today`, then `SELECT sum(total) FROM orders WHERE day = today`. Between them, another transaction commits three new orders.

steps.title: Fixing a lost update
steps.text:
There are three good ways, and none needs a stricter isolation level.

**Let the database do the arithmetic.** An update that computes from the current value is safe, because the database applies it to the latest committed row and makes a second writer wait for the first.

```sql
UPDATE products SET stock = stock - 1
WHERE id = 42 AND stock > 0;
```

If this reports that no row was updated, the item was out of stock. The check and the change are one atomic statement.

**Lock the row first.** `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE` reads the row and locks it until the transaction ends. A second transaction that does the same waits, and then reads the new value. Use this when the decision needs logic that cannot be put in one statement.

**Check a version.** Add a `version` column. Read it with the row, and write with `WHERE id = 42 AND version = 7`, increasing the version at the same time. If no row was updated, someone else changed it first, and the application reads again and retries. This is **optimistic locking**. It suits changes that take a long time between read and write, such as a person editing a form.

steps.title: Write skew
steps.text:
Write skew is harder to see, because the two transactions change different rows.

A hospital requires at least one doctor on call. Two doctors are on call and both want to leave. Each transaction checks that another doctor is on call, sees one, and marks its own doctor as off. Both commit. Nobody is on call.


Neither overwrote the other, so nothing detects a conflict at Read Committed or Repeatable Read. The same shape appears in "a room may not be double-booked", "a username must be unique" and "a team may have at most five members".

The fixes are:

- **A constraint**, where one can express the rule. A unique index prevents duplicate usernames outright, whatever the isolation level.
- **A lock on something both transactions share.** Lock the shift row, or the room row, with `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE` before checking. The second transaction waits and then sees the first one's change.
- **Serializable isolation.** The database detects that the two transactions could not have run one after the other with this result, and makes one of them fail.

steps.title: Serializable and retries
steps.text:
At Serializable, the database tracks what each transaction read and wrote. If a combination could not have come from running them one at a time, it aborts one with a serialization failure.

That is safe, and it moves work to the application, which must catch that specific error and run the whole transaction again. Code that uses Serializable without a retry loop will show users errors at random under load.

The same holds for Repeatable Read, which can fail with the same kind of error when two transactions update one row.

Retry the whole transaction from `BEGIN`, with new reads. Retrying only the failed statement reuses the old decisions.

steps.title: Which fix
steps.text: A booking system must not let two people reserve the same room for the same hour. Its code checks for an existing booking with a `SELECT`, and inserts a new row if none is found. It runs at Read Committed. Double bookings occur a few times a month.

steps.title: Exercise: name the anomaly
steps.text:
For each situation, name the anomaly and choose a fix. All run at Read Committed.

1. A wallet service reads a user's balance, adds a deposit in application code and writes the new balance. Two deposits arriving together sometimes result in only one being counted.
2. A coupon may be used 100 times in total. The code counts the uses with a `SELECT`, and inserts a new use if the count is below 100. The coupon has been used 103 times.
3. A monthly statement reads the opening balance, then the list of transactions, then the closing balance, in three statements. Sometimes they do not add up.
4. Two administrators edit the same product description in a form for ten minutes each. The one who saves second erases the other's changes.

steps.title: One possible answer
steps.text:
1. **Lost update.** Use `UPDATE wallets SET balance = balance + 25 WHERE id = ?`. The database computes from the current value, and a second update waits for the first.

2. **Write skew.** Each transaction inserts its own new row, so they never touch the same row, and each saw a count under 100. Lock the coupon row with `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE` before counting, so the checks happen one at a time. Or keep a `uses` column on the coupon and run `UPDATE coupons SET uses = uses + 1 WHERE id = ? AND uses < 100`, treating "no row updated" as "coupon exhausted".

3. **Non-repeatable read**, across statements. Run the three statements in one transaction at Repeatable Read, so they share a snapshot. It is a read-only transaction, so it will not fail with a conflict.

4. **Lost update, over a long time.** Locking a row for ten minutes while a person types would be wrong. Use a version column: the save succeeds only if the version is unchanged, and otherwise the second administrator is told that the text changed and shown the difference.

None of the four needed Serializable. The usual tools are an atomic update, a row lock, a constraint and a version check.

questions.prompt: What does the report show?

choices.text: A count and a sum for the same set of orders
choices.feedback: Each statement takes its own snapshot at this level.
