lessons.title: Locks and deadlocks
lessons.intro: When two transactions want to change the same thing, one has to wait. Locks are how the database arranges that. This module covers which locks are taken, how waiting turns into an outage, and how deadlocks arise and are avoided.

steps.title: What a lock is
steps.text:
A **lock** is a claim on a row or a table that lasts until the transaction ends. A transaction that needs a conflicting claim waits until the first one commits or rolls back.

You rarely ask for locks. Ordinary statements take them automatically.

- An `UPDATE` or `DELETE` locks each row it changes.
- A `SELECT` takes no row locks, thanks to row versions. Reads do not block writes, and writes do not block reads.
- Changing a table's structure takes a lock on the whole table.

The rule to remember is that locks are held until the end of the transaction, not until the end of the statement. A transaction that updates one row and then stays open for a minute holds that row for a minute.

steps.title: Row locks
steps.text:
Two transactions that update different rows do not affect each other. Two that update the same row run one after the other.


T2 does not fail. It waits. To the application, a wait looks like a slow query. That is why a lock problem is often reported as "the database is slow" when the processor and the disks are idle.

steps.title: Asking for a lock
steps.text:
Sometimes a transaction reads a row and will change it based on what it finds. To stop anyone else changing it in between, it locks the row while reading.

```sql
BEGIN;
SELECT * FROM seats WHERE id = 88 FOR UPDATE;   -- locks the row
-- decide in application code
UPDATE seats SET holder = 17 WHERE id = 88;
COMMIT;
```

Two options change what happens when the row is already locked.

- `FOR UPDATE NOWAIT` fails at once and does not wait.
- `FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED` passes over locked rows and returns the next free ones.

`SKIP LOCKED` is the standard way to build a job queue in a database table. Each worker selects the next unlocked job, so no two workers take the same one and none of them waits.

```sql
SELECT id FROM jobs
WHERE status = 'queued'
ORDER BY created_at
LIMIT 1
FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED;
```

steps.title: The queue behind a lock
steps.text:
Lock waits form queues. If T1 holds a row and T2 is waiting for it, T3 waits behind T2, and so on. One slow or forgotten transaction can leave hundreds of requests stuck behind it.

Table locks make this worse. A statement that needs to lock a whole table has to wait for every transaction that is using the table. While it waits, every new query on that table waits behind it. A change that would itself take 5 ms can stop all traffic to a table for as long as one old transaction stays open.

steps.title: Why did it stop
steps.text: At 14:00 every request that touches the `users` table starts to hang. Processor use on the database drops close to zero. At 14:00 a deploy ran a migration with `ALTER TABLE users ADD COLUMN ...`. A reporting query on `users` had been running since 13:40.

steps.title: Time limits on waiting
steps.text:
A wait with no limit is the dangerous part. Two settings bound it.

- A **lock timeout** makes a statement give up if it cannot get its lock within a set time. Set it before a schema change, so that a blocked migration fails after a few seconds and can be retried, and does not hold up the table.
- A **statement timeout** ends any statement that runs longer than a limit. It protects against runaway queries of every kind.

```sql
SET lock_timeout = '3s';
ALTER TABLE users ADD COLUMN locale text;
```

With that setting, the migration in the previous example would have failed after 3 seconds. Traffic would have paused for 3 seconds, not for 20 minutes.

steps.title: Deadlocks
steps.text:
A **deadlock** is two transactions that each hold a lock the other needs. Neither can continue, and waiting will never help.


The database checks for such cycles. When it finds one, it ends one of the transactions with a deadlock error, and the other proceeds. The application should treat that error like a serialization failure and retry the whole transaction.

A deadlock now and then is normal under load. Frequent deadlocks point to a design fault.

steps.title: Avoiding deadlocks
steps.text:
Deadlocks come from taking locks in different orders. The cures follow from that.

- **Lock in a fixed order.** If every transaction that touches two accounts locks the one with the lower ID first, a cycle cannot form. In the example, T2 would have asked for row 1 first and waited there, holding nothing.
- **Keep transactions short.** The less time locks are held, the smaller the chance of an overlap.
- **Touch fewer rows.** A statement that updates many rows takes its locks in whatever order it finds the rows. Two such statements can deadlock with each other.
- **Lock early.** Take every lock the transaction will need at its start, with `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE` in a fixed order, and then do the work.

steps.title: Optimistic and pessimistic
steps.text:
There are two attitudes to conflict.

**Pessimistic locking** assumes a conflict is likely and locks first: `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE`. Nobody else can change the row until you finish. It is right when conflicts are common and the work is short.

**Optimistic locking** assumes a conflict is unlikely and checks at the end. Read the row with its version number, do the work, and write only if the version is unchanged. No lock is held in between. It is right when conflicts are rare, or when the time between read and write is long.

| | Pessimistic | Optimistic |
| --- | --- | --- |
| When it acts | Before the work | When writing |
| On conflict | The second waits | The second fails and retries |
| Holds a lock meanwhile | Yes | No |
| Good for | Frequent conflicts, short work | Rare conflicts, long gaps |

steps.title: Seeing who is blocking whom
steps.text:
When things are stuck, the database can tell you why. PostgreSQL lists every connection, its state, how long its transaction has been open, and which other connection it is waiting for.

```sql
SELECT pid, state, wait_event_type, xact_start, query,
       pg_blocking_pids(pid) AS blocked_by
FROM pg_stat_activity
WHERE state <> 'idle'
ORDER BY xact_start;
```

Look for the connection at the root: the one that blocks others and is itself not waiting. Very often it is idle in transaction, or it is one long query. Ending that one connection frees everything behind it.

steps.title: The transfer
steps.text: A transfer function locks the sender's account row, then the receiver's. Two transfers start together: one from account 5 to account 9, the other from account 9 to account 5.

steps.title: Exercise: unblock the system
steps.text:
During a busy afternoon, the checkout starts timing out. You run the query from the section above and see this.


The time is now 13:41. Say what is happening, what you would do right now, and what you would change so that it does not happen again.

steps.title: One possible answer
steps.text:
**What is happening.** Connection 4101 began a transaction at 13:02, updated product 7, and has done nothing since. It is idle in transaction, and it has held the lock on that row for 39 minutes. Product 7 is probably popular. Every checkout that includes it waits behind 4101, in a chain.

**Right now.** End connection 4101, with `SELECT pg_terminate_backend(4101)`. Its transaction is rolled back, the row lock is released, and the queue drains within seconds. Its uncommitted update is lost, which is correct, since it was never completed.

**So it does not happen again**

1. **Find the code that left the transaction open.** Something began a transaction, updated stock, and then waited or crashed without committing or rolling back. Likely causes are a network call inside the transaction or an error path with no rollback.
2. **Set `idle_in_transaction_session_timeout`**, for example to 30 seconds. The database then ends such a connection by itself.
3. **Set a lock timeout** for the checkout's statements, such as 2 seconds. A blocked checkout then fails quickly with a clear error and does not hang until the client gives up.
4. **Alert on the age of the oldest open transaction.** A transaction open for more than a minute in a system like this is nearly always a fault, and this one went unnoticed for 38 minutes.

The useful habit is to look for the root of the chain. Three connections were visibly stuck, and the cause was the fourth, which was doing nothing.

lessons.title: Change a schema safely
lessons.intro: A schema has to change while the application is running and the tables are full. This module covers which changes are quick and which lock a table, how to make a change in steps that the running code survives, and how to move large amounts of data.

steps.title: Why schema changes are risky
steps.text:
On an empty development database, every schema change is instant. On a production table with 200 million rows and constant traffic, the same statement can do three harmful things.

- **Lock the table.** Most structural changes need a lock on the whole table, as the locking module described. While it is held, nothing can read or write.
- **Rewrite the table.** Some changes make the database copy every row into a new file. On a large table that takes minutes or hours, with the lock held throughout.
- **Break the running code.** During a deploy, old and new versions of the application run at the same time. A change that only the new version understands breaks the old one.

A safe change avoids all three. That takes knowing which statements are cheap, and splitting the dangerous ones into steps.

steps.title: Migrations as files
steps.text:
A **migration** is a small script that makes one change to the schema. Migrations are kept in version control with the code, numbered in order, and applied by a tool that records which ones have run.

This gives every environment the same schema, built by the same steps, and makes each change reviewable. Review a migration as carefully as code, with one extra question: what does this statement do to a large, busy table?

steps.title: Cheap and expensive changes
steps.text:
In current PostgreSQL versions, these are quick, because they change only the table's description:

- Adding a nullable column.
- Adding a column with a constant default.
- Dropping a column. The data is left in place and ignored.
- Renaming a column or table. Quick for the database, and dangerous for the application.

These are slow or blocking on a large table:

- Changing a column's type, in most cases. Every row is rewritten.
- Adding a `NOT NULL` constraint the plain way. The whole table is scanned under a lock.
- Adding a foreign key or a `CHECK` constraint the plain way. Every row is checked under a lock.
- Creating an index the plain way. Writes to the table are blocked for the whole build.

Even a quick change needs its table lock for a moment. If it has to wait for a long-running query, everything queues behind it. So set a lock timeout before every schema change, and retry on failure.

```sql
SET lock_timeout = '3s';
ALTER TABLE orders ADD COLUMN note text;
```

steps.title: Building an index without blocking
steps.text:
A plain `CREATE INDEX` blocks every insert, update and delete on the table until it finishes. On a large table that is minutes of failed writes.

PostgreSQL offers a second form that does not block writes.

```sql
CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY orders_customer_id_idx
  ON orders (customer_id);
```

It takes longer and it cannot run inside a transaction. If it fails partway, it leaves behind an index marked invalid, which must be dropped before trying again. On a table with real traffic it is the form to use every time.

Dropping an index has the same pair: `DROP INDEX CONCURRENTLY`.

steps.title: Constraints in two steps
steps.text:
A constraint can be added without a long lock by separating "enforce it for new rows" from "check the existing rows".

```sql
-- step 1: quick. New and changed rows must satisfy it from now on.
ALTER TABLE orders
  ADD CONSTRAINT orders_total_positive CHECK (total >= 0) NOT VALID;

-- step 2: scans the table, without blocking normal reads and writes.
ALTER TABLE orders VALIDATE CONSTRAINT orders_total_positive;
```

Foreign keys work the same way. For `NOT NULL`, add a `CHECK (col IS NOT NULL) NOT VALID`, validate it, and then set `NOT NULL`. PostgreSQL uses the validated check and skips its own scan.

steps.title: Which statement is dangerous
Old code and new code run together
steps.text:
During a deploy, some servers run the old code and some run the new, for seconds or minutes. A rollback means the old code runs again after the schema has changed. So at every moment the schema must work for both versions.

That rules out changes that seem natural.

- **Renaming a column** breaks the old code at once. It still uses the old name.
- **Dropping a column** breaks any code that still reads it, including `SELECT *` mapped onto a fixed set of fields.
- **Adding a required column** breaks old code that inserts without it.

steps.title: Expand, migrate, contract
steps.text:
The safe pattern splits one breaking change into steps that are each compatible with the code running at that moment.

1. **Expand.** Add the new thing beside the old. Nothing uses it yet.
2. **Migrate.** Deploy code that writes to both and reads from the old. Copy the existing data across. Then deploy code that reads from the new.
3. **Contract.** When nothing uses the old thing, remove it.

Renaming `users.fullname` to `users.display_name` becomes:


It is six steps where one statement would do on paper. Each of them is safe and can be undone, and there is never a moment when running code refers to something that does not exist.

steps.title: Backfills
steps.text:
Step 3 above is a **backfill**: filling a new column for rows that already exist. On a large table, one `UPDATE` of every row is a single huge transaction. It locks every row it touches until it ends, writes an enormous amount of log, makes replicas fall behind and bloats the table.

Do it in batches, as in the transactions module.

- Update a few thousand rows per transaction, selected by a range of primary keys.
- Pause briefly between batches, and watch replica lag and load.
- Make the job safe to stop and start again: `WHERE display_name IS NULL` skips rows already done.
- Keep the new code writing both columns while it runs, so that rows changed in the meantime stay correct.

```sql
UPDATE users SET display_name = fullname
WHERE id BETWEEN 1 AND 5000 AND display_name IS NULL;
-- then 5001 to 10000, and so on
```

steps.title: Changing a column's type
steps.text:
A type change that rewrites the table is handled with the same pattern, since a new column is a cheap change and a rewrite is not.

1. Add a new column of the new type.
2. Write to both from the application.
3. Backfill in batches.
4. Switch reads to the new column.
5. Drop the old column, and rename if you wish, in a later release.

steps.title: Migrations and deploys
steps.text:
Run schema changes separately from the code that needs them, and in the right order.

- A change that adds something goes out **before** the code that uses it.
- A change that removes something goes out **after** the code that stopped using it.

Avoid running migrations automatically when the application starts. With ten copies starting together, ten of them try to run the same migration. A slow migration then also delays the start of the application and can fail its health checks. Run migrations as their own step in the pipeline, once.

steps.title: Going back
steps.text:
Rolling a migration back is harder than rolling code back, because data has changed. A dropped column cannot be restored by a "down" script. Its values are gone.

So the plan for most schema changes is to move forward. Keep each step small and compatible, so the code can be rolled back while the schema stays. Delay the destructive step, the contract, until the new version has run long enough to be trusted. And take a backup or snapshot before any step that destroys data.

steps.title: The rename
steps.text: A team renames `orders.state` to `orders.status` with one `ALTER TABLE ... RENAME COLUMN`. The statement takes 4 ms. The new code, which uses `status`, is deployed over the following two minutes.

steps.title: Exercise: plan the change
steps.text:
An `accounts` table has 80 million rows and heavy traffic. It has a `plan` column of type text that holds `free`, `pro` or `team`. The team wants three changes.

1. A new required column `region`, which should be `'eu'` for all existing rows.
2. An index on `(region, plan)`.
3. A guarantee that `plan` can only hold one of the three values.

Write the steps in order, with the statement for each, and say what the application needs to do and when.

steps.title: One possible answer
steps.text:
**1. The new column**

```sql
SET lock_timeout = '3s';
ALTER TABLE accounts ADD COLUMN region text NOT NULL DEFAULT 'eu';
```

A constant default is stored in the table's description, so this is quick, and existing rows read as `'eu'` without being rewritten. Old code that inserts without `region` keeps working, because the default fills it in. Deploy this before the code that sets or reads `region`.

**2. The index**

```sql
CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY accounts_region_plan_idx
  ON accounts (region, plan);
```

It runs outside a transaction. Afterwards, check that the index is valid. If the build failed, drop the invalid index and run it again.

**3. The constraint**

First check for bad values, since validation will fail if any exist:

```sql
SELECT plan, count(*) FROM accounts GROUP BY plan;
```

Fix whatever turns up, in batches. Then:

```sql
ALTER TABLE accounts ADD CONSTRAINT accounts_plan_valid
  CHECK (plan IN ('free', 'pro', 'team')) NOT VALID;

ALTER TABLE accounts VALIDATE CONSTRAINT accounts_plan_valid;
```

**Order and code.** Each statement is its own migration, with a lock timeout and a retry. None needs a matching code change at the same moment, which is the point. One thing to tell the team: once the constraint exists, adding a fourth plan value means changing the constraint before the code that writes the value.

lessons.title: Connections and pools
lessons.intro: An application talks to its database over connections, and there are never as many of them as people assume. This module covers what a connection costs, how a pool shares a few among many requests, and how the way an application asks its questions matters as much as the questions.

steps.title: What a connection costs
steps.text:
Opening a connection is expensive. There is a TCP handshake, usually a TLS handshake, authentication, and in PostgreSQL the start of a whole operating-system process on the server to serve it. That takes several milliseconds at best, which is often longer than the query that follows.

Each open connection also uses memory on the database server, whether it is busy or not. For that reason a database has a hard limit on connections. PostgreSQL's default is 100, and raising it far does not help, because hundreds of processes competing for a few processors make everything slower.

So connections are a scarce resource. A system with 40 application servers cannot let each one open 50.

steps.title: The pool
steps.text:
A **connection pool** keeps a small set of connections open and lends them out. Code that needs the database borrows a connection, uses it and gives it back.

- No handshake per request. The connection is already open.
- The total is capped, so the database is never asked for more than it can serve.
- When every connection is lent out, the next request waits in line.

Nearly every database library has a pool built in. It may be on by default with a size you never chose.

steps.title: How big should a pool be
steps.text:
The instinct is to make the pool large so that nothing waits. That is usually wrong.

A database server can do only as much work at once as it has processor cores and disk capacity. Give it 16 queries on 8 cores, and each runs at half speed. Give it 200, and it spends its effort switching between them. Total throughput goes down.

A small pool that keeps the database busy and not overloaded finishes more work per second than a large one. A common starting point is a total, across all application servers, of a few times the number of processor cores on the database. Then measure and adjust.

The arithmetic matters when there are many servers. The total is the pool size multiplied by the number of application copies, plus background workers, scheduled jobs and people with consoles open.

steps.title: A proxy pool in front of the database
steps.text:
When many application copies each keep a pool, the totals add up quickly. A **connection proxy**, such as PgBouncer, sits between the applications and the database. Applications open as many connections as they like to the proxy, and the proxy shares a small number of real database connections among them.

It is most effective when it hands a database connection to a client for the length of one transaction and then takes it back. The cost is that anything tied to one connection across transactions no longer works as before, such as session settings.

Managed database services often offer such a proxy as a feature.

steps.title: Running out
steps.text: A service has a pool of 10 connections. A new endpoint opens a transaction, calls an external API that takes 5 seconds, and then commits. It receives 4 requests a second.

steps.title: Hold a connection briefly
steps.text:
A borrowed connection is unavailable to everyone else until it is returned. The rules are the same as for transactions.

- Borrow as late as possible and return as early as possible.
- Never hold a connection across a network call, a file upload or any slow work.
- Always return it, on the error paths too. A connection that is borrowed and never returned is a **leak**. After enough leaks the pool is empty, and the application hangs with no error.

Set a timeout for borrowing. A request that cannot get a connection within a second or two should fail with a clear error, and not wait until the user's request has long since timed out.

**Pool exhaustion** often looks like a slow database when the database is nearly idle. If queries are fast on the server and requests are slow in the application, measure the time spent waiting for a connection.

steps.title: One query per item
steps.text:
The most common performance fault in application code is the **N+1 problem**. The code fetches a list with one query, and then runs one more query for each item in the list.


Each query is fast, so the database's slow query log shows nothing. The time is in the round trips. With 500 items, or with a database 20 ms away, a page takes seconds.

The fault hides best behind libraries that load related data when a property is first read. A loop that looks like plain property access is running a query on every pass.

Count the queries a page makes. A number that grows with the size of the list is the sign.

steps.title: Ask only for what you need
steps.text:
Three smaller habits reduce work on both sides.

- **Name the columns.** `SELECT *` fetches every column, including large ones that the code ignores, and it prevents index-only scans.
- **Limit the rows.** A list that shows 20 rows should fetch 20, not 10,000 with the rest dropped in code.
- **Let the database do the set work.** Counting, summing and filtering belong in SQL. Fetching every row to count them in application code moves a great deal of data for one number.

steps.title: Paging through results
steps.text:
A long list is shown one page at a time. There are two ways to ask for a page.

**By offset.** `LIMIT 20 OFFSET 40000`. It is simple and it allows jumping to any page. The cost is that the database must produce and discard the first 40,000 rows to reach the ones you want. Deep pages get steadily slower.

**By key.** Remember the last row of the previous page and ask for the rows after it.

```sql
SELECT id, created_at, subject FROM tickets
WHERE created_at < '2025-03-04 10:15:00'
ORDER BY created_at DESC
LIMIT 20;
```

With an index on the sort column, this goes straight to the right place, so page 2,000 costs the same as page 1. It cannot jump to an arbitrary page, and the sort column needs a tie-breaker, such as the ID, when values can repeat.

Use paging by key for anything long or frequently scrolled.

steps.title: Parameters, not pasted text
steps.text:
Send values to the database as **parameters**, separate from the SQL text.

```sql
-- the statement, with a placeholder
SELECT * FROM users WHERE email = $1;
-- the value is sent separately: 'ana@example.com'
```

There are two reasons. The first is safety. Building SQL by pasting user input into a string lets a user change the meaning of the statement. This is **SQL injection**, one of the oldest and most damaging kinds of attack. A parameter is always treated as a value and never as SQL. The second is speed: the database can reuse its work for a statement it has seen before.

Use parameters every time, without exception. This is general guidance, not a statement of any organization's policy.

steps.title: Deep pages
steps.text: An admin screen pages through 5 million log rows with `ORDER BY id LIMIT 50 OFFSET n`. Page 1 loads in 3 ms.

steps.title: Exercise: find the waste
steps.text:
A "team activity" page is slow. Its code does this for a team of 60 members.

1. Opens a new database connection, with no pool.
2. Runs `SELECT * FROM members WHERE team_id = ?`.
3. For each member, runs `SELECT * FROM events WHERE member_id = ? ORDER BY created_at DESC` and keeps the first 5 rows in code.
4. For each of those events, runs `SELECT name FROM projects WHERE id = ?`.
5. Builds the SQL in step 2 by joining the team ID from the URL into the string.
6. Closes the connection.

List the problems. Estimate the number of queries. Then describe how the page should fetch its data.

steps.title: One possible answer
steps.text:
**Problems**

- **A new connection per page view** (steps 1 and 6). Every view pays for the handshakes and a new server process. Use a pool.
- **N+1, twice** (steps 3 and 4). 60 queries for events, then up to 300 for projects.
- **Fetching everything to keep five** (step 3). A member with 20,000 events has all of them sent to the application, which keeps 5.
- **`SELECT *`** throughout, when a few columns are shown.
- **SQL injection** (step 5). A value from the URL is pasted into the statement. This is the most serious item on the list.

**Query count.** 1 + 60 + 300 = 361 queries, plus a connection setup. At 1 ms of round trip each, that is over a third of a second in waiting alone.

**Better**

1. Borrow a pooled connection.
2. One query for the members, with the team ID as a parameter, naming the columns needed.
3. One query for the latest 5 events of all 60 members. In PostgreSQL, a lateral join does it: for each member, a subquery with `ORDER BY created_at DESC LIMIT 5`. An index on `events (member_id, created_at)` lets each of those read 5 entries.
4. Join `projects` in the same query, or fetch the distinct project IDs with one `IN` query.
5. Return the connection.

That is two or three queries. The page's time no longer depends on the size of the team or on how much history each member has.

choices.text: Nothing. Only the new endpoint is slow
choices.feedback: The new endpoint holds connections that every other endpoint needs.

choices.text: Within a few seconds all 10 connections are held by requests waiting on the API, and every other endpoint waits for a connection
choices.feedback: Each request keeps a connection for 5 seconds, and 4 arrive per second, so 20 are wanted at any time. The pool has 10. Endpoints that never call the API time out waiting.

choices.text: The pool grows to meet the demand
choices.feedback: A pool has a fixed maximum. That limit is the reason it exists.

questions.prompt: What happens at page 80,000, where the offset is 4 million?

choices.text: The same 3 ms, since only 50 rows are returned
choices.feedback: The rows returned are few. The rows skipped are many.

choices.text: It takes far longer, since the database walks past 4 million rows first
choices.feedback: An offset does not jump. The database reads and discards every row before it. Asking for `WHERE id > last_seen_id` goes straight there.

choices.text: It fails, since the offset is too large
choices.feedback: It works. It is only slow.

lessons.title: Keep a database healthy
lessons.intro: A database that is left alone gets slower. Dead rows pile up, statistics go out of date, and tables grow past what was planned. This module covers the routine work that prevents that: cleanup, statistics, watching queries, backups and old data.

steps.title: Dead rows and vacuum
steps.text:
An update writes a new version of a row and leaves the old one behind, and a delete only marks a row. Those leftover versions are **dead rows**. They take up space in table pages and index pages, and every scan has to step over them.

**Vacuum** is the process that reclaims them. It marks the space of dead rows as free, so new rows can reuse it. PostgreSQL runs it automatically in the background, table by table, when enough rows have changed. That is **autovacuum**.

Two points are often misunderstood.

- Vacuum makes space reusable inside the table. It does not usually shrink the file on disk. A table that bloated to 100 GB stays 100 GB, with free space inside it.
- Vacuum can only remove a dead row when no open transaction could still need to see it. One transaction left open for hours stops cleanup for the whole database.

steps.title: Bloat
steps.text:
**Bloat** is the gap between the size of a table and the size of its live data. Some is normal. Trouble starts when cleanup cannot keep up.

Common causes:

- **A long-running or idle transaction** that holds back cleanup, as described above.
- **Very heavy updates** on one table, faster than autovacuum's default settings handle. Busy tables often need autovacuum set to run more eagerly.
- **A mass delete or update**, which creates millions of dead rows at once.

The effects are slower scans, since more pages are read for the same rows, a larger memory footprint and more disk. An index can bloat too.

Shrinking a badly bloated table means rewriting it. `VACUUM FULL` does that, and it locks the table completely for the duration, so it is rarely acceptable on a live system. Tools exist that rebuild a table in the background and swap it in. Preventing bloat is much cheaper than removing it.

steps.title: The table that kept growing
steps.text: A `jobs` table holds about 50,000 live rows at any time. Rows are inserted, updated several times and deleted within minutes. After a month the table is 60 GB. A connection from an analytics tool has been "idle in transaction" for three weeks.

steps.title: Statistics
steps.text:
The planner chooses plans from statistics about each table: row counts, distinct values, common values. They are gathered by `ANALYZE`, which samples the table. Autovacuum runs it automatically after enough changes.

Statistics go stale in predictable situations.

- After a bulk load or a mass delete. The table has changed completely, and the planner still believes the old numbers.
- On a table that grows by appending. The newest rows, such as today's date, lie beyond the range the statistics know about, so the planner expects no rows for today.
- On a newly created or restored table before the first analyse has run.

The symptom is a query that was fast and suddenly has a bad plan, with estimated rows far from the actual rows. Running `ANALYZE` on the table by hand after any large data change is cheap and avoids this.

steps.title: Find the queries that matter
steps.text:
You cannot tune what you cannot see. Two tools show where a database spends its time.

A **slow query log** records every statement that takes longer than a threshold, such as 500 ms. It finds the single slow queries.

**Query statistics** add up every execution by statement shape. In PostgreSQL this is the `pg_stat_statements` extension. It shows, for each kind of query, how many times it ran and the total time it took.

The second is the more important. The query that costs the most is often not the slowest one. A 2 ms query that runs 5,000 times a second uses far more of the database than a 30-second report that runs once a night.


Sort by total time and work from the top.

steps.title: What to watch
steps.text:
A short list of measurements covers most database trouble.

| Measurement | Warns of |
| --- | --- |
| Connections in use against the limit | Running out, pool sizing errors |
| Age of the oldest open transaction | Stuck transactions, blocked cleanup |
| Queries waiting for locks | Lock queues |
| Replication lag | Stale reads, a failover that would lose data |
| Disk space free | The most final failure of all |
| Cache hit ratio | Data no longer fitting in memory |
| Dead rows per table | Cleanup falling behind |

Disk space deserves its own alert well ahead of time. A database with a full disk stops accepting writes, and recovering takes far longer than adding space would have.

steps.title: Backups
steps.text:
Replication protects against a failed machine. It does not protect against a wrong statement, which is copied to every replica within a second. A **backup** is a copy of the data from an earlier time, kept apart from the running system.

There are two kinds.

- A **logical backup** is a dump: the SQL statements or data files needed to recreate the database. It is portable and can restore one table. It is slow for large databases, both to take and to restore.
- A **physical backup** is a copy of the database's files, together with the write-ahead log. It is fast for large databases. With the log kept continuously, it allows **point-in-time recovery**: restoring to any chosen second, such as the moment before a bad `DELETE`.

Decide how much data you can afford to lose and how long a restore may take. Those two numbers choose the method. Then test it: restore a backup into a scratch environment on a schedule and check the data. A backup that has never been restored is not known to work.

steps.title: Old data
steps.text:
Many tables only ever grow: events, logs, audit records. Every query, index, backup and restore gets slower as they do. A plan for old data should exist before the table is large.

- **Retention.** Decide how long each kind of data is needed. Delete or archive the rest on a schedule.
- **Delete in batches**, as in the transactions module. One giant delete creates millions of dead rows and a huge transaction.
- **Partition by time.** The table is split into one piece per month or per day. Queries for a date range read only the pieces they need. Removing an old month means dropping its piece, which is instant and leaves no dead rows.

steps.title: Routine checks
steps.text:
A healthy database is the result of small, regular attention.

- Review the top queries by total time, monthly.
- Look for unused and duplicate indexes, and drop them.
- Check table and index sizes against their growth.
- Test a restore.
- Keep the database version supported. Old versions stop receiving security fixes.

steps.title: After the import
steps.text: A nightly job loads 30 million rows into a table that held 2 million. The morning dashboard query on that table, which took 200 ms yesterday, takes 90 seconds today. Its plan shows a nested loop with `rows=40` estimated and `rows=2800000` actual.

steps.title: Exercise: write the care plan
steps.text:
A team runs one PostgreSQL database for a busy scheduling product. They report these problems.

1. The `audit_log` table is 400 GB and grows by 30 GB a month. Rules require that 12 months be kept.
2. The `appointments` table is 5 times larger than its live data.
3. Nobody knows which queries use the most resources.
4. Backups are taken nightly. Nobody has ever restored one.
5. Last month the disk filled up and the product was down for two hours.

Write a plan that addresses each. Put the items in the order you would do them, and say why.

steps.title: One possible answer
steps.text:
**First: the things that can cause an outage or data loss**

- **Disk (5).** Add an alert at 70% and at 85% of disk used, and one on the projected days until full. This takes an hour and prevents a repeat.
- **Backups (4).** Restore last night's backup into a scratch environment now. Measure how long it takes and check recent data. Then schedule that test monthly. Turn on continuous archiving of the write-ahead log, so that a restore can go to a chosen minute and not only to last night.

**Second: visibility**

- **Queries (3).** Enable `pg_stat_statements` and a slow query log at 500 ms. Review the top ten by total time. This will probably explain some of the other problems.

**Third: the tables**

- **Bloat (2).** Find the cause before treating it. Check for long or idle transactions, and set `idle_in_transaction_session_timeout`. Then make autovacuum more eager for this table. Rebuild the table with a background tool in a quiet period, not with `VACUUM FULL`.
- **Audit log (1).** Partition it by month. That is a migration: create the partitioned table, write to it, and move the history across in batches. Afterwards, each month the oldest piece beyond 12 months is exported to cheap storage if required, and dropped. The table levels off at about 360 GB and stops growing.

The order follows risk. A full disk or an unrestorable backup can end the business. A bloated table makes it slower.

choices.text: Autovacuum is switched off
choices.feedback: It may be running constantly and finding nothing it is allowed to remove.

choices.text: The three-week-old transaction prevents every dead row created since then from being removed
choices.feedback: Vacuum may not remove a version that an open transaction might still read. Everything since that transaction began has to be kept.

choices.text: 50,000 rows take 60 GB
choices.feedback: Live data of that size would be a few megabytes. The rest is dead versions.

choices.text: Add an index
choices.feedback: The indexes are the same as yesterday. The plan changed because the planner's picture of the table is wrong.

choices.text: Run `ANALYZE` on the table, and add it as the last step of the import job
choices.feedback: The statistics still describe a table of 2 million rows. With fresh ones the planner sees the real sizes and chooses a suitable join.

choices.text: Increase the server's memory
choices.feedback: The plan is wrong for the data. More memory does not correct an estimate.

lessons.title: Find and fix a slow query
lessons.intro: This module puts the earlier ones together into one method. Given a query that is too slow, it shows what to check, in which order, and how to tell that a fix worked.

steps.title: The method
steps.text:
Use the same steps every time.

1. **Measure.** Get the exact query, with real values, and its real time.
2. **Decide whether the time is in the database.** It may be in round trips, in waiting for a connection or in waiting for a lock.
3. **Read the plan.** Find the step that takes the time.
4. **Name the cause.** One of a short list.
5. **Change one thing.**
6. **Measure again**, with the same values.

Skipping step 1 or step 6 is how people "fix" a query that was never the problem, or add an index that changes nothing.

steps.title: Step 1: get the real query
steps.text:
A report such as "the orders page is slow" is not a query. Find the SQL that is sent, and the values it is sent with. A query that is fast for an ordinary customer can be slow for the largest one.

Sources for the real query: the slow query log, the query statistics from the maintenance module, or the application's own tracing.

Run it yourself and note the time. Run it twice, since the first run may include reading pages from disk.

steps.title: Step 2: is the time in the database
steps.text:
Compare the time the database reports for the query with the time the application measures around it.

| Database says | Application says | The time is in |
| --- | --- | --- |
| 3 ms | 900 ms, across 300 queries | Round trips. An N+1 pattern |
| 3 ms | 2,000 ms, for one query | Waiting for a pooled connection, or the network |
| 4,000 ms, mostly waiting | 4,000 ms | A lock. Find the blocker |
| 4,000 ms, working | 4,000 ms | The query itself. Read the plan |

Only the last row is a query tuning problem. The others are solved in the application, the pool or the transaction that holds the lock, and no index will help them.

steps.title: Where is the time
steps.text: A page takes 1.4 seconds. The database's statistics show that the page's queries average 2 ms each. The application's trace shows 480 database calls for one page view.

steps.title: Step 3: read the plan
steps.text:
Run `EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS)` with the slow values, and look for these, in order.

1. **The step with the most time**, remembering to multiply by `loops`.
2. **Rows removed by a filter.** A step that reads far more rows than it keeps.
3. **Estimated against actual rows.** A large gap means the planner was misled.
4. **Sorts and hashes that went to disk.** Marked by "external merge" or by several batches.
5. **Pages read.** A large `read` count means the data was not in memory.

One of these nearly always points at the cause.

steps.title: Step 4: the usual causes
steps.text:
Most slow queries have one of a small number of causes, each with a matching fix.

| Sign in the plan | Cause | Fix |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Seq Scan, many rows removed by filter | No usable index | Add an index on the filtered column |
| Index exists and is not used | The column is wrapped in a function, the types differ, or a leading column is skipped | Rewrite the condition, or index the expression |
| Sort of many rows before a small LIMIT | The index does not give the order | A composite index: equality columns, then the sort column |
| Nested loop with huge `loops` | A bad row estimate | Run `ANALYZE`. Check for skewed data |
| Inner side of a join is a Seq Scan | The foreign key column has no index | Index it |
| Index Scan with many heap fetches | Too many rows visited | A covering index, or return fewer rows |
| Everything is simply large | The query asks for too much | Page it, summarise it, or precompute it |

The last row is a different kind of answer. Some queries are slow because they do a great deal of legitimate work. No index makes "total every order since 2015" cheap. Those are handled by asking for less, or by keeping a summary.

steps.title: Step 5: change one thing
steps.text:
Make one change and test it. If you add two indexes, rewrite the query and raise a memory setting all at once, you will not know which change helped, and you will keep all of them, including the ones that only add cost.

Test an index on a copy of production data when you can. A test database with a thousand rows will choose a different plan from one with a hundred million, so results from small data tell you little.

Build new indexes with `CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY` on a live system.

steps.title: Step 6: measure again
steps.text:
Run the same query with the same values and compare the plans. Check that:

- the slow step is gone or changed,
- the time dropped by the amount you expected,
- the pages read went down.

Then check what the change cost. A new index slows writes to that table. Look at the insert and update times of the busiest write paths afterwards. Check the other slow value too: a plan that suits the largest customer should not make the ordinary case worse.

steps.title: A worked example
steps.text:
A support screen lists a customer's 20 most recent tickets and takes 3 seconds for large customers.

```sql
SELECT id, subject, status, created_at
FROM tickets
WHERE customer_id = 9001
ORDER BY created_at DESC
LIMIT 20;
```


Reading it: the index on `customer_id` is used, which is good. It finds all 410,000 tickets of this customer, visiting 388,000 pages on disk. Then all of them are sorted to keep 20. The index finds the customer and does not give the order.

The fix is one composite index, with the equality column first and the sort column second.

```sql
CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY tickets_customer_created_idx
  ON tickets (customer_id, created_at DESC);
```


The `Sort` is gone. The scan reads 20 entries, already in order, and stops. 388,000 pages became 24. The old index on `customer_id` alone is now redundant and can be dropped, which gives back the write cost that the new one added.

steps.title: When the query is not the problem
steps.text:
Some slow queries cannot be fixed by tuning, because they should not run in that form.

- **A report on the live database at peak time.** Move it to a replica, or to a summary table built overnight.
- **A count of everything.** An exact `count(*)` over a huge table reads the whole table. Ask whether an estimate, a stored counter or "more than 10,000" would do.
- **A search with a leading wildcard.** `LIKE '%word%'` reads every row. Use a full-text index.
- **A page that shows everything.** Add paging.

The most effective tuning question is often whether the query needs to do this much work at all.

steps.title: Settings come last
steps.text:
Database settings, such as memory per sort or the size of the buffer cache, matter. They are the last thing to change, not the first.

A missing index makes a query a thousand times slower. A setting changes it by a small factor. Raising a memory limit to make a bad plan bearable also raises it for every other query, which can exhaust the server's memory under load. Fix the queries and the indexes first.

steps.title: Which cause
steps.text: A library generates the condition `WHERE account_id::text = '4411'`, which converts the column to text before comparing. The column `account_id` is a number, and it has an index. The plan shows a sequential scan of 60 million rows.

steps.title: Exercise: tune it
steps.text:
An "unread notifications" badge runs this query on every page view, about 2,000 times a second. It averages 180 ms.

```sql
SELECT count(*) FROM notifications
WHERE user_id = ? AND read_at IS NULL;
```

The table has 900 million rows. There is one index, on `user_id`. A typical user has 4,000 notifications, of which 3 are unread. The plan shows an index scan on `user_id` returning about 4,000 rows, a filter on `read_at` that removes nearly all of them, and around 3,800 pages touched.

Work through the method. Say where the time goes, propose a fix, and say how you would check it. Then propose a second change that questions the query itself.

steps.title: One possible answer
steps.text:
**Where the time goes.** The time is in the database, in the query's own work. The index finds all 4,000 of the user's notifications. Each one needs a visit to the table to check `read_at`, and those rows are scattered over about 3,800 pages. All of that work keeps 3 rows. The sign is "rows removed by filter", which is large compared with the rows kept.

**The fix.** A partial index that holds only unread notifications.

```sql
CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY notifications_unread_idx
  ON notifications (user_id) WHERE read_at IS NULL;
```

Nearly all 900 million rows are read, so this index is tiny by comparison, perhaps a thousandth of the full one. For a user with 3 unread notifications it holds 3 entries, and counting them touches a few pages. It can also be answered as an index-only scan.

**Checking it.** Run `EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS)` again for the same user. The plan should name the new index, the filter line should be gone, and the pages touched should fall from about 3,800 to under 10. Then watch the query's mean time in the statistics over a day, and check that marking a notification as read has not become slower. It should not, since that update now removes one small index entry.

**Questioning the query.** A badge does not need an exact, fresh count 2,000 times a second. Two options: cache the count per user for 30 seconds, or keep an `unread_count` column on the `users` table that is changed when notifications are created and read, with a periodic repair job. And the badge could show "9+" beyond nine, so that the query can stop early with a `LIMIT`.

Try the index first. It is one statement, it is easy to undo, and it will probably make the rest unnecessary.

choices.feedback: It is as selective as a condition can be. The index is being bypassed for another reason.

lessons.title: Review a schema and its queries
lessons.intro: This module has no new ideas. You review a schema and the code that uses it, read a plan, and then design a schema of your own. Do each exercise on paper before you read its answer.

steps.title: How to use this module
steps.text:
Each exercise has a step where you work alone and a step with one possible answer. The answers are not the only good ones. Compare your reasoning with them, and pay most attention to anything you did not think of at all.

When you review a database design, ask the same questions each time.

1. Is each fact stored once, with a constraint that keeps it valid?
2. Does each frequent query have an index that fits it, and is any index unused?
3. Which code reads a value and then writes based on it?
4. How long is each transaction open, and what does it hold?
5. What happens to this table when it is a hundred times larger?

steps.title: Review 1: a booking system
steps.text:
A small gym built this. Read the schema and the description of the code, and list every problem you find. Rank them.

```sql
CREATE TABLE bookings (
  id           serial,
  member_name  text,
  member_email text,
  class_name   text,
  class_time   text,          -- for example '2025-03-04 18:00'
  price        float,
  paid         text,          -- 'yes' or 'no'
  tags         text           -- for example 'yoga,beginner'
);
CREATE INDEX ON bookings (member_name);
CREATE INDEX ON bookings (class_name);
CREATE INDEX ON bookings (tags);
CREATE INDEX ON bookings (paid);
```

The code works like this:

- To book: it counts the bookings for the class with a `SELECT`. If the count is below 20, it inserts a new row.
- The "my bookings" page runs `SELECT * FROM bookings WHERE lower(member_email) = ?`, then loops over the rows and runs one query per row to fetch the class description from another table.
- Paying opens a transaction, sets `paid = 'yes'`, calls the payment provider and commits when the provider answers.
- The SQL for the class search is built by joining the search text into the query string.

steps.title: The most urgent one
steps.text: Before you read the full list, choose from three of the faults.

steps.title: Review 1: what is wrong
steps.text:
**Security**

1. **SQL injection** in the class search. Send the search text as a parameter. This is general guidance, not a statement of any organization's policy.

**Correctness**

2. **Overbooking.** Count-then-insert is write skew. Two bookings can both see 19 and both insert. Lock the class row with `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE` before counting, or keep a `spots_taken` column and use `UPDATE ... SET spots_taken = spots_taken + 1 WHERE spots_taken < 20`.
3. **No primary key and no constraints.** `serial` does not make a column a key. Nothing is `NOT NULL`. Nothing stops the same member from booking the same class twice.
4. **`price` as `float`.** Money needs an exact decimal type.
5. **`class_time` as text.** It cannot be compared, sorted or checked properly. Use a timestamp with time zone.
6. **`paid` as text.** Use a boolean, or a `paid_at` timestamp that is empty until payment.

**Design**

7. **Members and classes are repeated in every booking.** A member's email is stored once per booking, so it cannot be changed safely. A class with no bookings cannot exist. Split the table into `members`, `classes` and `bookings`.
8. **`tags` is a list in one column.** It belongs in its own table, one row per tag.

**Performance**

9. **`lower(member_email)` cannot use an index**, and there is none on the email anyway. With a `members` table, the page looks up bookings by `member_id`.
10. **N+1** on the "my bookings" page. Join the classes in one query.
11. **Four weak indexes.** `paid` has two values. `tags` holds a list as text. Replace them with indexes that match real queries: `bookings (member_id)`, `bookings (class_id)`.
12. **`SELECT *`** where four columns are shown.

**Transactions**

13. **A network call inside the transaction.** The row is locked, and a connection is held, for as long as the payment provider takes. Mark the booking as pending, commit, call the provider, and record the result in a second transaction.

steps.title: Review 2: a plan
steps.text:
The gym's weekly report takes 40 seconds. It lists each class in the past 7 days with its number of bookings. Here is the query and its plan, after the schema was split into three tables.

```sql
SELECT c.name, count(b.id)
FROM classes c
JOIN bookings b ON b.class_id = c.id
WHERE c.starts_at >= now() - interval '7 days'
GROUP BY c.name;
```


Find the step that takes the time, explain why, and say what to change. Say whether the sequential scan on `classes` needs fixing.

steps.title: Review 2: what the plan says
steps.text:
**Where the time goes.** The inner `Seq Scan on bookings` takes about 470 ms and runs 85 times: 85 times 472 ms is 40 seconds. That is the whole query.

**Why.** For each of the 85 classes, the database scans all 2.6 million bookings to find about 20. The join column `bookings.class_id` is a foreign key, and PostgreSQL did not create an index for it.

**The fix.**

```sql
CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY bookings_class_id_idx
  ON bookings (class_id);
```

Each inner step becomes an index scan that reads a few pages. The query should drop from 40 seconds to a few milliseconds. The same index speeds up every other query that finds bookings by class, including the capacity check.

**The scan on `classes`.** It reads 4,385 rows in about 1 ms. It is not worth fixing today. An index on `starts_at` becomes worthwhile when the table is far larger. The estimate there was accurate, 90 against 85, so the statistics are fine.

The method is the one from the tuning module: multiply by `loops`, find the step with the time, and look for rows removed by a filter.

steps.title: Design: a library of shared documents
steps.text:
Design the schema for a document-sharing product. Users belong to one or more workspaces. A workspace has folders, and a folder can contain other folders and documents. A document has a title, a body that can be very large, and a history of versions. A document can be shared with individual users, with "view" or "edit" permission. The product must show a workspace's 50 most recently edited documents quickly, and must never lose an edit when two people save at once.

Write the tables with keys, types and constraints. List the indexes with the query each one serves. Say how concurrent saves are handled, and name one thing you would denormalize and one you would not.

steps.title: Design: one possible answer
steps.text:
**Tables**

```sql
CREATE TABLE users (
  id     bigint GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY,
  email  text NOT NULL UNIQUE,
  name   text NOT NULL
);

CREATE TABLE workspaces (
  id    bigint GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY,
  name  text NOT NULL
);

CREATE TABLE memberships (
  workspace_id  bigint NOT NULL REFERENCES workspaces (id),
  user_id       bigint NOT NULL REFERENCES users (id),
  PRIMARY KEY (workspace_id, user_id)
);

CREATE TABLE folders (
  id            bigint GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY,
  workspace_id  bigint NOT NULL REFERENCES workspaces (id),
  parent_id     bigint REFERENCES folders (id),
  name          text NOT NULL
);

CREATE TABLE documents (
  id            bigint GENERATED ALWAYS AS IDENTITY PRIMARY KEY,
  workspace_id  bigint NOT NULL REFERENCES workspaces (id),
  folder_id     bigint NOT NULL REFERENCES folders (id),
  title         text NOT NULL,
  version       integer NOT NULL DEFAULT 1,
  edited_at     timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now()
);

CREATE TABLE document_versions (
  document_id  bigint  NOT NULL REFERENCES documents (id),
  version      integer NOT NULL,
  body         text    NOT NULL,
  author_id    bigint  NOT NULL REFERENCES users (id),
  created_at   timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),
  PRIMARY KEY (document_id, version)
);

CREATE TABLE shares (
  document_id  bigint NOT NULL REFERENCES documents (id),
  user_id      bigint NOT NULL REFERENCES users (id),
  permission   text   NOT NULL CHECK (permission IN ('view', 'edit')),
  PRIMARY KEY (document_id, user_id)
);
```

Choices worth noting: the many-to-many relationships (`memberships`, `shares`) are tables with a composite primary key, which also prevents duplicates. A folder's `parent_id` is empty for a top-level folder. The large `body` lives in `document_versions`, so listing documents never reads it.

**Indexes**

| Index | Serves |
| --- | --- |
| `documents (workspace_id, edited_at DESC)` | The 50 most recently edited documents of a workspace, in order, with no sort |
| `documents (folder_id)` | Listing a folder |
| `folders (workspace_id, parent_id)` | Listing a folder's subfolders |
| `memberships (user_id)` | A user's workspaces. The primary key starts with `workspace_id`, so it does not serve this |
| `shares (user_id)` | "Shared with me" |

The primary keys already serve "members of a workspace", "shares of a document" and "one version of a document".

**Concurrent saves.** Optimistic locking with the `version` column. A person may edit for minutes, so holding a lock is wrong. A save runs in one transaction:

```sql
UPDATE documents
SET version = version + 1, edited_at = now()
WHERE id = ? AND version = ?;   -- the version the editor started from
```

If one row was updated, insert the new `document_versions` row and commit. If none was, someone else saved first. Roll back and show the editor the newer version. No edit is overwritten silently, and the primary key on `(document_id, version)` refuses a duplicate version as a second line of defence.

**Denormalized.** `documents.workspace_id` repeats what the folder already says, and `documents.edited_at` repeats the newest version's timestamp. Both exist so that the "recent documents" query is one index scan on one table. Both are written in the same transaction as the change they mirror.

**Not denormalized.** The author's name on each version. Joining `users` by primary key for 50 rows costs almost nothing, and a copied name would have to be updated across every version when a user renames themselves.

steps.title: What to check before a release
steps.text: A team is about to ship a feature that adds a column, a new query on a 300-million-row table, and a function that reads a balance and then updates it.

steps.title: Where to go next
steps.text:
You can now explain what a query costs, choose indexes for it, read its plan, design tables that protect their own data, and reason about what happens when many transactions run at once.

Four habits are worth keeping.

- **Look at the plan** before and after every change, with real values on real-sized data.
- **Let the database enforce the rules.** A constraint holds when the code does not.
- **Be suspicious of read-then-write.** Make it one statement, lock the row, or check a version.
- **Keep transactions short**, and never wait on anything outside the database while one is open.

The details in this course are PostgreSQL's. When you work with another database, the ideas carry over and the particulars need checking: its default isolation level, which schema changes lock a table, and how it cleans up old rows.

questions.prompt: Which fault would you fix first?

choices.text: The four single-column indexes
choices.feedback: They cost writes and help little. Nobody is harmed by them today.

choices.text: The search that joins user text into the SQL string
choices.feedback: It is SQL injection. Anyone who can use the search box can read or change the whole database. The fix is to send the text as a parameter.

choices.text: The price stored as a floating-point number
choices.feedback: It causes small rounding errors in totals. That needs fixing, and it is not an open door.

questions.prompt: Which check is most likely to prevent an incident?

choices.text: Confirm that the tests pass on the development database
choices.feedback: They will pass. A development database has a few hundred rows, so every plan is fast and no two transactions overlap.

choices.text: Read the plan of the new query on production-sized data, check what the migration locks, and look for read-then-write code
choices.feedback: These are the three things that behave differently at production size and under real concurrency.

choices.text: Add indexes on every column the new query mentions
choices.feedback: Indexes chosen without a plan cost writes and may not be used.
